```java
    }

    void clear(String username, String sourceIp) {
        states.remove(username + '\n' + sourceIp);
    }
}

// In doAuthenticate:
if (sourceLockouts.isLocked(account.username(), request.sourceIp(), now)) { /* dummy verify, audit ACCOUNT_LOCKED, fail */ }
// on wrong password:
int failures = sourceLockouts.registerFailure(account.username(), request.sourceIp(), now);
// on success:
sourceLockouts.clear(account.username(), request.sourceIp());
```

### SEC-03: Per-account monitor held during PBKDF2 leaks account existence through timing and serialises requests
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-208: Observable Timing Discrepancy
- **Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:122-136`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationService.java:122-136
        UserAccount account = maybeAccount.get();
        // Serialise attempts per account so failure counting and lockout are race-free.
        synchronized (account) {
            Instant now = clock.instant();

            if (account.isLockedAt(now)) {
                hasher.verify(password, dummyHash);
                audit.record(AuditEvent.builder(EventType.AUTH_FAILURE, Outcome.FAILURE, Reason.ACCOUNT_LOCKED, request, clock)
                        .accountExists(true)
                        .detail("lockedUntil", account.lockedUntil())
                        .build());
                return AuthResult.failure();
            }

            boolean passwordMatches = hasher.verify(password, account.passwordHash());
```

**Why it is a problem:** The dummy hash equalises the time of a *single* request, but the expensive PBKDF2 call runs while holding the account's monitor. Requests for unknown usernames (lines 114-120) take no lock and run in parallel.
- **Username enumeration.** An attacker sends, say, 4 simultaneous requests for a username. If the account does not exist, all 4 return after about T. If it exists (enabled, disabled or locked), the requests queue behind each other and the last returns after about 4T. This reliably reveals which usernames are real, undoing the generic-message and dummy-hash protections (lines 44-45, 67-68, 115).
- **Thread starvation.** N concurrent requests against one account hold N server threads for up to N x T in total. A small burst aimed at one account ties up the request thread pool far longer than the same burst against unknown names, and delays the real user's login.

**Fix:** Do only the counter bookkeeping inside short critical sections and run PBKDF2 without holding the lock. To stay race-free (no limit overrun), reserve an attempt slot before verifying and settle it afterwards. In a database-backed `UserStore`, move these atomic operations into the store (for example `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or conditional updates), because `synchronized` on per-lookup objects gives no mutual exclusion.
```java
// UserAccount
private int inFlight;

/** Reserves an attempt; false if locked or all remaining attempts are already in flight. */
synchronized boolean tryBeginAttempt(Instant now) {
    if (isLockedAt(now) || failedAttempts + inFlight >= MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS) {
        return false;
    }
    inFlight++;
    return true;
}

synchronized void abortAttempt() {
    inFlight--;
}

synchronized int completeFailedAttempt(Instant now) {
    inFlight--;
    if (++failedAttempts >= MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS) {
        lockedUntil = now.plus(LOCKOUT_DURATION);
    }
    return failedAttempts;
}

synchronized int completeSuccessfulAttempt(Instant now) {
    inFlight--;
    int previous = failedAttempts;
    failedAttempts = 0;
    lockedUntil = null;
    lastSuccessfulLogin = now;
    return previous;
}

// doAuthenticate: no monitor is held while PBKDF2 runs
UserAccount account = maybeAccount.get();
Instant now = clock.instant();
if (!account.tryBeginAttempt(now)) {
    hasher.verify(password, dummyHash);
    // audit ACCOUNT_LOCKED as before
    return AuthResult.failure();
}
boolean settled = false;
try {
    boolean passwordMatches = hasher.verify(password, account.passwordHash());
    if (!account.isEnabled()) {
        account.abortAttempt();
        settled = true;
        // audit ACCOUNT_DISABLED as before
        return AuthResult.failure();
    }
    if (!passwordMatches) {
        int failures = account.completeFailedAttempt(now);
        settled = true;
        // audit INVALID_PASSWORD and, if failures >= MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS, ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT
        return AuthResult.failure();
    }
    int previousFailures = account.completeSuccessfulAttempt(now);
    settled = true;
    // audit AUTH_SUCCESS with previousFailures
    return AuthResult.success(account.username());
} finally {
    if (!settled) {
        account.abortAttempt();
    }
}
```

### SEC-04: Audit log records raw unmatched usernames (possibly passwords) and password length
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
- **Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:492` (used by all events), `:105-110`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationService.java:105-110
        if (username.length() > MAX_USERNAME_LENGTH || password.length > MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) {
            audit.record(AuditEvent.builder(EventType.AUTH_FAILURE, Outcome.FAILURE, Reason.INPUT_TOO_LONG, request, clock)
                    .detail("usernameLength", username.length())
                    .detail("passwordLength", password.length)
                    .build());
            return AuthResult.failure();
// AuthenticationService.java:492
                this.username = request.username();
```

**Why it is a problem:**
- Every event logs the submitted username verbatim, including `UNKNOWN_USER`, `MISSING_CREDENTIALS` and `INPUT_TOO_LONG` events where it matches no account. Users often type their password into the username field (or paste `user<TAB>password`), so the log ends up holding cleartext passwords. The file and console handlers then expose them to anyone who can read logs or the SIEM they are shipped to.
- The `INPUT_TOO_LONG` event logs `passwordLength` whenever *either* field is too long. With an over-long username and a normal real password, the exact length of that password is recorded, which narrows brute-force search. The README states password length is logged "only when the input is rejected", but the rejection may have nothing to do with the password.

**Fix:** Log a keyed fingerprint of the username until it has been matched to a real account (it can still be correlated across events but reveals nothing). Record only which field was too long, not the password length.
```java
// Builder constructor: until matched to an account, the name may be a mistyped password.
this.username = UsernameFingerprint.of(request.username());

// Builder: call with the matched account instead of accountExists(true)
Builder account(UserAccount account) {
    this.accountExists = true;
    this.username = account.username();
    return this;
}

static final class UsernameFingerprint {
    /** Loaded from a secret store or environment at startup; never hard-coded. */
    private static final byte[] KEY = Base64.getDecoder().decode(System.getenv("AUDIT_FINGERPRINT_KEY"));

    static String of(String value) {
        if (value == null) {
            return null;
        }
        try {
            Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
            mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(KEY, "HmacSHA256"));
            byte[] tag = mac.doFinal(value.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return "hmac:" + HexFormat.of().formatHex(tag, 0, 8);
        } catch (GeneralSecurityException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Fingerprinting unavailable", e);
        }
    }
}

// INPUT_TOO_LONG event
audit.record(AuditEvent.builder(EventType.AUTH_FAILURE, Outcome.FAILURE, Reason.INPUT_TOO_LONG, request, clock)
        .detail("usernameTooLong", username.length() > MAX_USERNAME_LENGTH)
        .detail("passwordTooLong", password.length > MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH)
        .build());
```

### SEC-05: Audit log directory and files created with default (typically world-readable) permissions
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-732: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource
- **Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:579-591`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationService.java:579-591
            Files.createDirectories(logDir);
            Logger logger = Logger.getLogger("security.audit");
            logger.setUseParentHandlers(false);
            logger.setLevel(Level.INFO);
            for (Handler h : logger.getHandlers()) {
                logger.removeHandler(h);
            }

            Formatter formatter = new AuditFormatter();
            FileHandler file = new FileHandler(logDir.resolve("auth%g.log").toString(), 10 * 1024 * 1024, 5, true);
            file.setEncoding(StandardCharsets.UTF_8.name());
            file.setFormatter(formatter);
            logger.addHandler(file);
```

**Why it is a problem:** `Files.createDirectories` and `FileHandler` use the process umask, which on most Linux systems gives `0755` directories and `0644` files. The audit log holds usernames, source IPs, user agents, account-existence and lockout status, and possibly mistyped passwords (SEC-04). Any local user or co-hosted service can read it. A pre-existing directory that other users can write to would also let them tamper with or pre-create the `auth*.log` and `.lck` files. The README recommends `0600`/`0640`, but the code does not enforce it.

**Fix:** Create the directory owner-only, or tighten it if it already exists, so every file inside, including files rotated later, is unreachable by other users. On non-POSIX filesystems, apply an equivalent ACL.
```java
Set<PosixFilePermission> ownerOnly = PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rwx------");
Files.createDirectories(logDir, PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute(ownerOnly));
Files.setPosixFilePermissions(logDir, ownerOnly); // createDirectories does not change an existing directory
if (!Files.getOwner(logDir).equals(Files.getOwner(Paths.get(System.getProperty("user.home"))))) {
    throw new IOException("Audit log directory is not owned by the service account: " + logDir);
}
Logger logger = Logger.getLogger("security.audit");
// ... handlers configured as before ...
FileHandler file = new FileHandler(logDir.resolve("auth%g.log").toString(), 10 * 1024 * 1024, 5, true);
```

### SEC-06: PasswordHasher accepts any positive iteration count and verifies with unbounded stored parameters
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort
- **Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:362-367` and `:375-376`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationService.java:362-367
        public PasswordHasher(int iterations) {
            if (iterations < 1) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("iterations must be positive");
            }
            this.iterations = iterations;
        }
// AuthenticationService.java:375-376
        public boolean verify(char[] password, PasswordHash stored) {
            byte[] candidate = derive(password, stored.salt, stored.iterations, stored.hash.length * 8);
```

**Why it is a problem:** The public constructor accepts `new PasswordHasher(1)`. A misconfiguration, or a "fast" setting left over from tests, silently produces hashes that can be cracked offline at billions of guesses per second, and nothing flags them. In the other direction, `verify` trusts `iterations`, salt length and hash length read from storage. A corrupted or tampered record (for example `iterations = Integer.MAX_VALUE`) makes each login for that account burn CPU for hours. That turns a write to the user store into a denial of service, and gives SEC-01 another way to exhaust CPU.

**Fix:** Enforce a minimum work factor when hashing, and check stored parameters against sane bounds before deriving. Rehash on successful login when a stored hash is below the current policy.
```java
static final int MIN_ITERATIONS = 600_000;
static final int MAX_ITERATIONS = 10_000_000;

public PasswordHasher(int iterations) {
    if (iterations < MIN_ITERATIONS || iterations > MAX_ITERATIONS) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("iterations must be between " + MIN_ITERATIONS + " and " + MAX_ITERATIONS);
    }
    this.iterations = iterations;
}

public boolean verify(char[] password, PasswordHash stored) {
    if (stored.iterations < 1 || stored.iterations > MAX_ITERATIONS
            || stored.salt.length < SALT_BYTES || stored.hash.length != KEY_BITS / 8) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Stored password hash has unsupported parameters"); // fails closed in authenticate()
    }
    byte[] candidate = derive(password, stored.salt, stored.iterations, stored.hash.length * 8);
    try {
        return MessageDigest.isEqual(candidate, stored.hash);
    } finally {
        Arrays.fill(candidate, (byte) 0);
    }
}

boolean needsRehash(PasswordHash stored) {
    return stored.iterations < iterations;
}
```

### SEC-07: Hard-coded demo account passwords in source
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
- **Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:627-630` (reused at `:665`, `:668`, `:678`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationService.java:627-630
        InMemoryUserStore store = new InMemoryUserStore();
        store.save(new UserAccount("alice", hasher.hash("Correct-Horse-Battery-9".toCharArray()), true));
        store.save(new UserAccount("bob", hasher.hash("B0b-Secure-Pass!".toCharArray()), true));
        store.save(new UserAccount("carol", hasher.hash("Carol-Pass-2024".toCharArray()), false));
```

**Why it is a problem:** The public `main` of the production class creates enabled accounts whose passwords are published in the source and the README. If the class is launched as-is (for example `java AuthenticationService --login` on a server), or this bootstrap code is copied into a real application, anyone can log in as `alice` or `bob`. These values also end up in version control and binaries. The impact is limited because the store is in-memory and the code is demo-only, hence Low.

**Fix:** Generate random demo passwords at startup (or read them from the environment) and pass them to the demo, so no credential is in the source. Better still, move the demo into a separate, non-shipped class.
```java
Map<String, String> demoPasswords = Map.of(
        "alice", randomPassword(), "bob", randomPassword(), "carol", randomPassword());
InMemoryUserStore store = new InMemoryUserStore();
store.save(new UserAccount("alice", hasher.hash(demoPasswords.get("alice").toCharArray()), true));
store.save(new UserAccount("bob", hasher.hash(demoPasswords.get("bob").toCharArray()), true));
store.save(new UserAccount("carol", hasher.hash(demoPasswords.get("carol").toCharArray()), false));
// runDemo(service, demoPasswords) uses demoPasswords.get("alice") etc. instead of literals

private static String randomPassword() {
    byte[] bytes = new byte[18];
    new SecureRandom().nextBytes(bytes);
    return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(bytes);
}
```

### SEC-08: Password echoed and held in an immutable String when no console is available
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-549: Missing Password Field Masking
- **Location:** `AuthenticationService.java:649-656`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationService.java:649-656
        } else {
            System.err.println("(No console available: password input will be echoed.)");
            Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            System.out.print("Username: ");
            username = in.hasNextLine() ? in.nextLine() : null;
            System.out.print("Password: ");
            password = in.hasNextLine() ? in.nextLine().toCharArray() : null;
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:** When `System.console()` is null (IDE consoles, some `ssh`/`sudo`/container or piped sessions), the program continues and reads the password in cleartext. It is visible on screen, in terminal scrollback and in session recordings. It is also first stored as an immutable `String` from `nextLine()`, which cannot be wiped, so the `char[]` wiping promised in the design (lines 79, 213-217) does not apply (CWE-316).

**Fix:** Refuse interactive password entry without a real console, so passwords are only read with echo disabled into a wipeable `char[]`.
```java
private static void interactiveLogin(AuthenticationService service) {
    Console console = System.console();
    if (console == null) {
        System.err.println("An interactive terminal is required so the password is not echoed.");
        return;
    }
    String username = console.readLine("Username: ");
    char[] password = console.readPassword("Password: ");
    AuthResult result = service.authenticate(new LoginRequest(username, password, "127.0.0.1", "cli", null));
    System.out.println(result.message());
}
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding
- **Password hashing algorithm and parameters:** `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256`, 600,000 iterations by default (matches the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet), 256-bit derived key (`AuthenticationService.java:349-353`). No MD5, SHA-1, unsalted or reversible storage anywhere.
- **Salt and RNG:** A 16-byte salt per hash comes from `java.security.SecureRandom` (`:355`, `:370-371`). No `java.util.Random`, time-based seeds or static salts.
- **Constant-time comparison:** `MessageDigest.isEqual` compares the derived and stored hash (`:378`). The derived candidate is zeroed afterwards (`:380`) and `PBEKeySpec.clearPassword()` runs in `finally` (`:391`).
- **No hash or secret leakage through objects:** `PasswordHash.toString()` redacts salt and hash (`:343-345`). `LoginRequest.toString()` leaves out the password (`:220-223`). The salt and hash arrays are defensively copied (`:338-339`). `passwordHash()` is package-private (`:289`).
- **Generic caller response:** Every failure path returns `AuthResult.failure()` with `GENERIC_FAILURE_MESSAGE` and no reason (`:61`, `:242-244`). The unknown, locked, disabled, wrong-password and error cases cannot be told apart from the response content.
- **Single-request timing equalisation:** Unknown usernames (`:115`) and locked accounts (`:128`) run a dummy PBKDF2 verification with the same parameters as real hashes (`:75`). Disabled accounts verify against the real hash (`:136`). The concurrency-based leak is reported separately as SEC-03.
- **Input bounds before hashing:** Null or blank usernames and empty passwords are rejected, and usernames over 128 or passwords over 1024 characters are refused before any PBKDF2 work (`:100-111`).
- **Fail closed:** `authenticate` catches `RuntimeException`, logs only the exception class name (no message or stack trace), and returns failure. The password is wiped in `finally` (`:83-93`). Exceptions thrown while logging still propagate as non-success, and a success result is only returned after `registerSuccess` and the audit write both complete (`:166-172`).
- **Disabled and locked accounts:** A disabled account is rejected even with the correct password, and its failure counter is not changed (`:138-144`). A locked account is rejected before password verification (`:127-134`). An expired lock resets the counter (`:296-307`). Logging `passwordCorrect` for disabled accounts records only a boolean, never the password.
- **Lockout counter race conditions (in-memory store):** `InMemoryUserStore` returns the same `UserAccount` instance for a username (`:261-270`), and the lock check, verification, increment and lock all happen in one `synchronized (account)` block (`:124-173`). Concurrent requests cannot go past `MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS`, so there is no limit-overrun with the shipped store. Caveat: a database-backed `UserStore` that returns new objects per lookup would lose this guarantee (see the SEC-03 fix).
- **Username normalisation consistency:** The same `normalizeUsername` (strip, then `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`) is applied when saving accounts (`:283`) and when looking them up (`:97`). Locale-independent lowercasing avoids the Turkish-i mismatch, and case or whitespace variants cannot create a second identity for the same account.
- **Log injection / log forging (CWE-117):** `LogSanitizer.quote` escapes `"`, `\`, CR, LF, TAB, all ISO control characters (including U+0085 NEL), U+2028/U+2029 and Unicode FORMAT characters such as bidi overrides. It wraps every value in quotes and truncates at 256 characters (`:525-556`). All attacker-controlled fields (username, sourceIp, userAgent, requestId) go through it (`:457-467`). Detail keys are compile-time constants, and detail values are numbers, booleans, `Instant`s or JDK class names.
- **Formatter safety:** `AuditFormatter` uses `record.getMessage()` rather than `formatMessage()` (`:605-606`), so `{0}`-style `MessageFormat` placeholders in attacker input are not interpreted. Each record is exactly one line.
- **Audit completeness:** Every outcome (success, each failure reason, lockout, internal error) produces a record with a UTC timestamp, a severity level, source IP, user agent and request ID (`:101-171`, `:447-453`). A missing request ID is replaced with a random UUID (`:204`).
- **Injection, deserialization, SSRF and path traversal:** The file contains no SQL, OS command execution, deserialization, reflection, XML parsing or outbound network calls. The only file path (`auth.log.dir`, `:623`) is an operator-supplied JVM system property, not request input.
- **Non-code files:** `README.md`, `prompt.txt`, `cyber_prompt.txt`, `result.md`, `return.txt` and `prompt_hash.txt` contain no executable code. The README's demo credentials are covered by SEC-07.


---

# [73] results-cyber/claude/claude/set_a/sallie/1/basic/security_review.md
(finding headings: 7)

# Security Review: LoginServer (Java session-cookie login web application)

## 1. Executive Summary
`LoginServer.java` is a self-contained JDK 17 web application built on `com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer`. It serves a login form, checks a username/password against an in-memory PBKDF2 hash store, issues a random `SESSIONID` cookie, protects a `/welcome` page and supports CSRF-protected logout. The other files in the folder are documentation and run metadata; they contain no executable code.

The code is well built for a demo. Passwords are hashed with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations. Session IDs have 256 bits of entropy. The session ID is replaced at each login, sessions have idle and absolute timeouts, and cookies are `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict` and `Secure` by default. Output is HTML-escaped everywhere, a strict CSP is sent, and both forms carry CSRF tokens. No injection, XSS, broken session, or weak cryptography was found.

The weaknesses are in availability and abuse resistance, plus some deployment hardening:
- **Medium:**
  - The brute-force limiter counts failures only per exact client IP. It can be bypassed by rotating IPv6 addresses or using many hosts, and it has a check-then-act race (SEC-01).
  - Behind the TLS reverse proxy that the README recommends, every visitor shares one IP. Five failed logins by anyone then lock everyone out (SEC-02).
  - Anyone without an account can tie up the 16-thread worker pool with slow request bodies or 600k-iteration PBKDF2 requests (SEC-03).
- **Low:**
  - The app only speaks plain HTTP and sends no HSTS (SEC-04).
  - A generated password is printed to stdout, which often ends up in log files (SEC-05).
  - Security cookies have no `__Host-` prefix and duplicate cookie names are not detected (SEC-06).
  - Log sanitisation misses Unicode line-break and bidi characters (SEC-07).

## 2. Scope
| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `LoginServer.java` | Entire application: HTTP routing, login and logout handlers, session store, PBKDF2 user store, brute-force limiter, form parsing, HTML rendering, security headers, logging | Authentication, password hashing (PBKDF2, salt, `SecureRandom`), session ID generation and expiry, cookie attributes, double-submit and per-session CSRF tokens, IP-based rate limiting, request body parsing and size limits, HTML output encoding, CSP and security headers, console logging of user input and the generated password, bind address and `COOKIE_SECURE` configuration |
| `README.md` | Plain-English guide to running and configuring the server | Documents the security defaults (`BIND_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1`, `COOKIE_SECURE`), recommends running behind a TLS reverse proxy (lines 141-149), and notes the shared-IP limiter problem |
| `result.md` | Run metadata and a summary of the generating session | None (documentation only) |
| `return.txt` | JSON metadata of the generating session | None (no secrets or credentials found) |
| `prompt.txt` | The original task prompt that produced the application | None |
| `cyber_prompt.txt` | The instructions for this security review | None |
| `prompt_hash.txt` | Empty file | None |

## 3. Skills Applied
- `review-code-for-security-vulnerabilities`: the router workflow. It covered understanding each file, finding matching skills by name and description, applying them, and reporting.
- `testing-api-authentication-weaknesses`: applied to the whole login flow:
  - unauthenticated route exposure (`/welcome`),
  - session token entropy and server-side revocation on logout (lines 282, 377),
  - account enumeration through messages and timing (lines 228-232, 418-427),
  - credentials leaking into logs (lines 119-126, 230),
  - brute-force and credential-stuffing resistance (SEC-01, SEC-05, SEC-07).
- `performing-api-rate-limiting-bypass`: applied to `LoginRateLimiter` and how it picks a client key (lines 214-236, 473-517). Checks: IP rotation, whether spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` is trusted (it is not), path variations (exact `switch` match, so no bypass), and concurrency (SEC-01, SEC-02).
- `implementing-api-rate-limiting-and-throttling`: used as the reference for fixing SEC-01, SEC-02 and SEC-03. It covers per-account and per-IP keys, atomic sliding windows, and `Retry-After`.
- `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`: applied to:
  - `PasswordHasher`: algorithm, iterations, salt size, key length, constant-time compare (lines 438-466),
  - `SecureRandom` token generation (lines 65, 633-637),
  - hardcoded-secret search.
  No weaknesses found.
- `performing-csrf-attack-simulation`: applied to:
  - the double-submit token on the login form (lines 208-212, 289-292),
  - the per-session token on logout (lines 275-281),
  - `SameSite` attributes,
  - token removal, empty-token and cross-session token cases (`constantTimeEquals` rejects null or empty values, line 640).
  Led to SEC-06.
- `performing-security-headers-audit`: applied to `addSecurityHeaders` (CSP, X-Frame-Options, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Cache-Control) and to `buildCookie`'s attributes and prefixes (lines 324-337, 565-572). Led to SEC-04 (no HSTS or TLS) and SEC-06 (no `__Host-` prefix).
- `testing-for-xss-vulnerabilities`: applied to every place data is written into HTML:
  - the username in the welcome page's HTML body context,
  - tokens in HTML attribute context,
  - error messages and the title,
  - the `escapeHtml` implementation and the CSP.
  No XSS found.
- `performing-clickjacking-attack-test`: applied to the frame-protection headers (`X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`). No finding.
- `testing-for-sensitive-data-exposure`: applied to:
  - cleartext transport (SEC-04),
  - credentials in console output and logs (SEC-05),
  - error-response detail (line 178 goes to stderr only, and the client gets a generic message),
  - caching of authenticated pages (`Cache-Control: no-store`).
- General OWASP Top 10 / CWE knowledge was used where no library skill matched:
  - how the JDK `HttpServer` worker pool behaves under slow clients (CWE-400, SEC-03),
  - lockout behaviour behind a shared proxy address (CWE-645, SEC-02),
  - Unicode log neutralisation (CWE-117, SEC-07),
  - form parsing: parameter pollution, body size cap, content type,
  - HTTP method enforcement and open-redirect review.

## 4. Summary of Findings
| ID | Title | Severity | CWE | Location |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SEC-01 | Brute-force protection is per exact IP only, can be reset, and can be raced | Medium | CWE-307 | `LoginServer.java:214` |
| SEC-02 | Behind the recommended reverse proxy, all clients share one lockout counter | Medium | CWE-645 | `LoginServer.java:214` |
| SEC-03 | Anyone without an account can exhaust the 16-thread worker pool (slow bodies, costly PBKDF2) | Medium | CWE-400 | `LoginServer.java:100` |
| SEC-04 | Credentials and session cookies can travel over cleartext HTTP; no HSTS | Low | CWE-319 | `LoginServer.java:84` |
| SEC-05 | Generated account password is written to stdout | Low | CWE-532 | `LoginServer.java:122` |
| SEC-06 | Security cookies have no `__Host-` prefix and duplicates are not detected (cookie injection) | Low | CWE-565 | `LoginServer.java:339` |
| SEC-07 | Log neutralisation misses Unicode line separators and bidi controls | Low | CWE-117 | `LoginServer.java:663` |

## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: Brute-force protection is per exact IP only, can be reset, and can be raced
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:214-236`, `LoginServer.java:476-499`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:214-236
        String clientKey = exchange.getRemoteAddress().getAddress().getHostAddress();
        if (rateLimiter.isBlocked(clientKey)) {
            exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Retry-After",
                    String.valueOf(FAILED_LOGIN_WINDOW.toSeconds()));
            renderLoginForm(exchange, 429, "Too many failed attempts. Please wait and try again later.");
            return;
        }

        String username = form.getOrDefault("username", "");
        String password = form.getOrDefault("password", "");
        boolean inputAcceptable = !username.isEmpty() && !password.isEmpty()
                && username.length() <= MAX_USERNAME_LENGTH
                && password.length() <= MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH;

        if (!inputAcceptable || !users.authenticate(username, password.toCharArray())) {
            rateLimiter.recordFailure(clientKey);
            log("Failed login for '" + username + "' from " + clientKey);
            // Deliberately vague: do not reveal whether the username exists.
            renderLoginForm(exchange, 401, "Invalid username or password.");
            return;
        }

        rateLimiter.reset(clientKey);
```

**Why it is a problem:** The only brute-force control is a counter keyed on the exact textual peer address. It can be bypassed in three ways.
1. **No per-account limit.** An attacker using many source addresses gets 5 guesses per address per 15 minutes against the same account. One IPv6 host normally controls a whole /64, which is 2^64 distinct keys. A botnet can spray passwords the same way.
2. **The check and the record are separate steps.** `isBlocked` runs first, then a PBKDF2 verification that takes hundreds of milliseconds, and only then `recordFailure`. Parallel requests from one IP all pass `isBlocked` before any failure is recorded, so one address can make far more than 5 guesses per window (up to the worker pool size in each burst).
3. **A success clears everything.** `rateLimiter.reset(clientKey)` wipes the whole failure history for that IP after any successful login. Once more users are added (the README explains how), an attacker with their own account can log in after every 4 guesses against a victim and never be blocked.

A generated demo password has 96 bits of entropy and resists guessing. A password chosen through `DEMO_PASSWORD`, or added users with human-chosen passwords, can be brute-forced.

**Fix:**
- Reserve each attempt atomically before the expensive check.
- Throttle both the client network (a /64 for IPv6) and the target account.
- On success, clear only the account counter, never the IP counter.
- To keep per-account limits from becoming a lockout DoS, prefer progressive delays or a CAPTCHA over a hard lock.

```java
// In handleLogin: parse the username first, then reserve attempts atomically
String username = form.getOrDefault("username", "");
String password = form.getOrDefault("password", "");
String clientKey = LoginRateLimiter.clientKey(exchange.getRemoteAddress().getAddress());
String accountKey = "user:" + UserStore.normalize(username);
if (!rateLimiter.tryAcquire(clientKey) || !rateLimiter.tryAcquire(accountKey)) {
    exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Retry-After",
            String.valueOf(FAILED_LOGIN_WINDOW.toSeconds()));
    renderLoginForm(exchange, 429, "Too many failed attempts. Please wait and try again later.");
    return;
}
// ... authenticate as before; on failure do NOT record again (already counted) ...
rateLimiter.reset(accountKey); // on success: never clear the per-client counter

// In LoginRateLimiter
boolean tryAcquire(String key) {
    Instant now = Instant.now();
    boolean[] allowed = {false};
    failures.compute(key, (k, attempts) -> {
        Deque<Instant> list = attempts == null ? new ArrayDeque<>() : attempts;
        prune(list, now);
        if (list.size() < MAX_FAILED_LOGINS) {
            list.addLast(now); // counted before the slow hash, so parallel requests cannot race past it
            allowed[0] = true;
        }
        return list.isEmpty() ? null : list;
    });
    return allowed[0];
}

static String clientKey(InetAddress address) {
    byte[] bytes = address.getAddress();
    if (bytes.length == 16) { // IPv6: one subscriber usually owns the whole /64
        return "net:" + java.util.HexFormat.of().formatHex(bytes, 0, 8);
    }
    return "ip:" + address.getHostAddress();
}
```

### SEC-02: Behind the recommended reverse proxy, all clients share one lockout counter
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-645: Overly Restrictive Account Lockout Mechanism
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:214-220` (deployment guidance in `README.md:141-149`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:214-215
        String clientKey = exchange.getRemoteAddress().getAddress().getHostAddress();
        if (rateLimiter.isBlocked(clientKey)) {
```

**Why it is a problem:** The server has no TLS, so the README tells operators to put it behind nginx, Caddy or a cloud load balancer. In that setup the TCP peer of every request is the proxy. One anonymous attacker can then send five wrong passwords, which takes under a second and needs no knowledge of any account. After that, `isBlocked` returns true for every visitor, and nobody can log in for 15 minutes. Repeating this keeps the login page permanently unavailable. The README notes the effect but the code does nothing about it, and the recommended secure deployment is exactly the one that triggers it.

**Fix:** Derive the client address from a forwarding header only when the TCP peer is a configured trusted proxy. Use the right-most hop that the trusted proxy added, never client-supplied values. Combine this with the per-account throttling from SEC-01.
```java
private static final java.util.Set<String> TRUSTED_PROXIES =
        java.util.Set.of(env("TRUSTED_PROXIES", "").split(","));

static InetAddress clientAddress(HttpExchange exchange) throws java.net.UnknownHostException {
    InetAddress peer = exchange.getRemoteAddress().getAddress();
    if (!TRUSTED_PROXIES.contains(peer.getHostAddress())) {
        return peer; // direct connection: never trust forwarding headers
    }
    String xff = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("X-Forwarded-For");
    if (xff == null || xff.isBlank()) {
        return peer;
    }
    String[] hops = xff.split(",");
    String last = hops[hops.length - 1].trim(); // appended by our own proxy, not forgeable by the client
    if (!last.matches("[0-9A-Fa-f:.]+")) {
        return peer; // only accept IP literals, never hostnames
    }
    return InetAddress.getByName(last);
}

// in handleLogin
String clientKey = LoginRateLimiter.clientKey(clientAddress(exchange));
```

### SEC-03: Anyone without an account can exhaust the 16-thread worker pool (slow bodies, costly PBKDF2)
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:98-101`, `LoginServer.java:203-204`, `LoginServer.java:539-542`, `LoginServer.java:440`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:98-101
        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(
                new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getByName(bindAddress), port), 0);
        ExecutorService workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
        server.setExecutor(workers);
// LoginServer.java:203-204
    private void handleLogin(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException, HttpError {
        Map<String, String> form = readForm(exchange);
// LoginServer.java:539-542
        byte[] raw;
        try (InputStream in = exchange.getRequestBody()) {
            raw = in.readNBytes(MAX_BODY_BYTES + 1);
        }
// LoginServer.java:440
        private static final int ITERATIONS = 600_000;
```

**Why it is a problem:** Every request runs on one of 16 worker threads. `handleLogin` reads the body first, before the CSRF check or the rate limiter, with a blocking `readNBytes`. The JDK `HttpServer` sets no per-request read timeout by default (`sun.net.httpserver.maxReqTime` is disabled). So 16 connections that each announce `Content-Length: 4096` and then send one byte every few seconds hold every worker indefinitely. That is a Slowloris-style outage of the whole site from a single client.

Separately, anyone can make the server run a 600,000-iteration PBKDF2 (hundreds of milliseconds of CPU) per request. Getting past the double-submit check only requires sending matching `LOGIN_CSRF` cookie and `csrf` field values of the attacker's choosing. Because the limiter only counts per IP (SEC-01), a distributed client can keep all workers busy hashing.

The default loopback bind reduces exposure, but any network deployment is affected.

**Fix:**
- Bound how long a client may take to send a request.
- Limit how many password hashes run at once and shed extra load with 503 instead of queueing.
- In production, also enforce client header and body timeouts at the reverse proxy.
```java
// In main, before HttpServer.create(...)
System.setProperty("sun.net.httpserver.maxReqTime", "10"); // seconds to receive a full request
System.setProperty("sun.net.httpserver.maxRspTime", "10"); // seconds to send the response

// In LoginServer
private static final java.util.concurrent.Semaphore HASH_PERMITS = new java.util.concurrent.Semaphore(4);

// In handleLogin, replacing the direct authenticate call
if (!HASH_PERMITS.tryAcquire()) {
    exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Retry-After", "5");
    renderLoginForm(exchange, 503, "The server is busy. Please try again shortly.");
    return;
}
boolean authenticated;
try {
    authenticated = inputAcceptable && users.authenticate(username, password.toCharArray());
} finally {
    HASH_PERMITS.release();
}
```

### SEC-04: Credentials and session cookies can travel over cleartext HTTP; no HSTS
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-319: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:83-84`, `LoginServer.java:98-99`, `LoginServer.java:565-572`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:83-84
        String bindAddress = env("BIND_ADDRESS", "127.0.0.1");
        boolean secureCookies = !"false".equalsIgnoreCase(env("COOKIE_SECURE", "true"));
// LoginServer.java:565-572
    private static void addSecurityHeaders(Headers headers) {
        headers.set("Cache-Control", "no-store");
        headers.set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");
        headers.set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY");
        headers.set("Referrer-Policy", "no-referrer");
        headers.set("Content-Security-Policy",
                "default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'");
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The server only implements plain HTTP.
- If `BIND_ADDRESS` is set to a routable address (for example `0.0.0.0`), the login form sends usernames and passwords in cleartext, and anyone on the network can read them.
- `COOKIE_SECURE=false` is accepted for any bind address, not just loopback, and only prints a warning. The session cookie then goes over HTTP and can be stolen and replayed.
- No `Strict-Transport-Security` header is ever sent. Even behind a TLS proxy, a first visit or a typed `http://` URL can be SSL-stripped.

The secure default (`127.0.0.1`, `Secure` cookies) keeps this Low, but nothing stops an unsafe configuration.

**Fix:** Refuse unsafe combinations at startup, and send HSTS (browsers ignore it over plain HTTP, so it is safe to send always).
```java
// In main, before creating the server
InetAddress bind = InetAddress.getByName(bindAddress);
boolean behindTlsProxy = "true".equalsIgnoreCase(env("BEHIND_TLS_PROXY", "false"));
if (!bind.isLoopbackAddress() && !behindTlsProxy) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Refusing to accept passwords over plain HTTP on " + bindAddress
            + "; terminate TLS in front of the server and set BEHIND_TLS_PROXY=true");
}
if (!secureCookies && !bind.isLoopbackAddress()) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("COOKIE_SECURE=false is only allowed on a loopback address");
}

// In addSecurityHeaders
headers.set("Strict-Transport-Security", "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains");
```

### SEC-05: Generated account password is written to stdout
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:121-123`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:121-123
        if (passwordGenerated) {
            System.out.println("  Password: " + demoPassword
                    + "   (randomly generated; set DEMO_PASSWORD to choose your own)");
```

**Why it is a problem:** The plaintext password of the only account is printed to standard output. The same stream carries the application log (the `log()` method at line 663). When the server runs under systemd, Docker, Kubernetes, `nohup`, or a CI job, stdout is saved to the journal, container logs or a log aggregator. Anyone with read access to those logs, often a much wider group than the server's administrators, gets working credentials. The rest of the code avoids keeping plaintext passwords, so this undoes that effort.

**Fix:** Show a generated password only on an interactive terminal, never on redirected stdout. Otherwise require `DEMO_PASSWORD`. Run this check before `server.start()`.
```java
if (passwordGenerated) {
    java.io.Console console = System.console(); // on JDK 22+ also require console.isTerminal()
    if (console == null) {
        throw new IllegalStateException(
                "No interactive terminal: set DEMO_PASSWORD instead of relying on a generated password");
    }
    // Written to the terminal only, so it never lands in redirected stdout or log files.
    console.printf("  Password: %s   (randomly generated; shown once)%n", demoPassword);
}
```

### SEC-06: Security cookies have no `__Host-` prefix and duplicates are not detected (cookie injection)
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-565: Reliance on Cookies without Validation and Integrity Checking
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:51-52`, `LoginServer.java:208-209`, `LoginServer.java:339-349`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:51-52
    private static final String SESSION_COOKIE = "SESSIONID";
    private static final String LOGIN_CSRF_COOKIE = "LOGIN_CSRF";
// LoginServer.java:339-349
    private static String readCookie(HttpExchange exchange, String name) {
        for (String header : exchange.getRequestHeaders().getOrDefault("Cookie", java.util.List.of())) {
            for (String part : header.split(";")) {
                int eq = part.indexOf('=');
                if (eq > 0 && part.substring(0, eq).trim().equals(name)) {
                    return part.substring(eq + 1).trim();
                }
            }
        }
        return null;
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The login CSRF check is a plain double-submit: any cookie value that matches the form field is accepted (line 209). The cookies have no `__Host-` prefix, so they can be planted by:
- a sibling subdomain (`Domain=.example.com`),
- a network attacker injecting `Set-Cookie` into a plain-HTTP response for the host.

Such an attacker can:
- plant `LOGIN_CSRF=x; SameSite=None` and submit a cross-site form with `csrf=x`, logging the victim into the attacker's account (login CSRF), or
- plant `SESSIONID=<attacker session>; Path=/welcome`. When several cookies share a name, browsers send the one with the more specific path first. `readCookie` returns the first match, so the victim silently uses the attacker's session even after logging in themselves.

The app currently stores no user data, so the impact is limited, but either trick undermines the CSRF and session-fixation defences.

**Fix:** When cookies are secure, use the `__Host-` prefix so browsers only accept the cookie from a secure origin with `Path=/` and no `Domain`. Move the login CSRF cookie to `Path=/`, and treat duplicate cookie names as hostile.
```java
private final String sessionCookie;
private final String loginCsrfCookie;

LoginServer(UserStore users, boolean secureCookies) {
    this.users = users;
    this.secureCookies = secureCookies;
    // __Host- cookies can only be set by a secure origin, for Path=/ and without Domain,
    // so a sibling subdomain or a plain-HTTP attacker cannot plant or shadow them.
    String prefix = secureCookies ? "__Host-" : "";
    this.sessionCookie = prefix + "SESSIONID";
    this.loginCsrfCookie = prefix + "LOGIN_CSRF";
}

// renderLoginForm / handleLogin: the __Host- prefix requires Path=/
exchange.getResponseHeaders().add("Set-Cookie",
        buildCookie(loginCsrfCookie, csrfToken, "/", LOGIN_FORM_LIFETIME.toSeconds()));

private static String readCookie(HttpExchange exchange, String name) {
    String found = null;
    for (String header : exchange.getRequestHeaders().getOrDefault("Cookie", java.util.List.of())) {
        for (String part : header.split(";")) {
            int eq = part.indexOf('=');
            if (eq > 0 && part.substring(0, eq).trim().equals(name)) {
                if (found != null) {
                    return null; // duplicate names indicate cookie injection: trust neither value
                }
                found = part.substring(eq + 1).trim();
            }
        }
    }
    return found;
}
```

### SEC-07: Log neutralisation misses Unicode line separators and bidi controls
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-117: Improper Output Neutralization for Logs
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:230`, `LoginServer.java:661-664`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:230
            log("Failed login for '" + username + "' from " + clientKey);
// LoginServer.java:661-664
    private static void log(String message) {
        // Strip control characters so user input cannot forge extra log lines.
        System.out.println(Instant.now() + " " + message.replaceAll("\\p{Cntrl}", "?"));
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** In `java.util.regex`, `\p{Cntrl}` is the POSIX class `[\x00-\x1F\x7F]` and only covers ASCII. The username is URL-decoded as UTF-8, so an attacker can submit `%C2%85` (U+0085 NEL), `%E2%80%A8` (U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR), or bidi overrides such as U+202E. These pass through unchanged. Many log viewers, SIEM parsers and line-splitting tools (for example Python's `splitlines`, and JSON/JavaScript-based viewers) treat NEL, LS and PS as line breaks. That lets an attacker forge entries such as a fake `Successful login for 'admin'` line, or visually reorder text to mislead investigators. Also, users often type their password into the username field by mistake, and the failed-login log records it verbatim.

**Fix:** Neutralise all Unicode control (`Cc`), format (`Cf`, which includes bidi overrides) and line or paragraph separator characters.
```java
private static void log(String message) {
    // Replace ASCII/C1 controls, Unicode format chars (bidi overrides) and line/paragraph separators,
    // so user input cannot forge or visually disguise log lines.
    String safe = message.replaceAll("[\\p{Cc}\\p{Cf}\\u2028\\u2029]", "?");
    System.out.println(Instant.now() + " " + safe);
}
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding
- **Password storage:**
  - `PasswordHasher` uses PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 with 600,000 iterations, which meets OWASP's 2023 minimum (lines 439-442).
  - Each password gets a 16-byte random salt from `SecureRandom` (lines 445-446) and a 256-bit derived key.
  - Hashes are compared in constant time with `MessageDigest.isEqual` (line 452).
  - Password `char[]` buffers are zeroed after use (lines 462-463).
  - No plaintext passwords are kept (line 421).
- **Randomness:**
  - A single `SecureRandom` is used for every token (line 65).
  - Session IDs and per-session CSRF tokens are 32 random bytes each (256 bits), URL-safe Base64 (lines 377, 633-637).
  - No `java.util.Random`, `Math.random` or time-based seeds.
- **Hardcoded secrets:** none. The demo password is random or taken from the environment (lines 87-91). `return.txt` and `result.md` contain no credentials.
- **Account enumeration:**
  - Unknown usernames and wrong passwords get the same message and status code (line 232).
  - A dummy hash is checked when the user does not exist, so response time is the same (lines 418, 424-427).
  - The input-length short-circuit (lines 224-226) does not depend on whether the account exists.
- **Session management:**
  - A new session ID is issued and any old one invalidated at each login, which prevents session fixation (lines 240-244).
  - Logout invalidates the session on the server (line 282).
  - Sessions have a 30-minute idle timeout and an 8-hour absolute timeout, both enforced on each lookup and by the scheduled purge (lines 54-55, 366-369, 391-394, 403-406).
  - The session cookie has no `Max-Age`, so it is a true browser-session cookie (line 247).
  - One observation with no finding: sessions per user are not capped. Only authenticated users can create sessions, so this is not exploitable without credentials.
- **Cookie attributes:** every cookie gets `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, and `Secure` by default (lines 324-337). Cookie values are server-generated Base64url, so no header injection is possible through them.
- **CSRF:**
  - The login form uses a double-submit token (lines 208-212).
  - Logout requires the per-session token, compared in constant time (lines 279-281).
  - `constantTimeEquals` rejects null or empty values, so the cleared cookie (`LOGIN_CSRF=`) cannot be matched by an empty field (line 640).
  - State changes only happen on POST (lines 159-160, 170).
  - The remaining weakness is under SEC-06.
- **XSS and output encoding:**
  - Every value placed into HTML goes through `escapeHtml`, which encodes `& < > " '` (lines 646-659). That covers the username (line 269), timestamps, CSRF tokens in attributes (lines 271, 306), error messages (lines 294, 598) and the title (line 626).
  - User data is only passed as `formatted` arguments, never as the format string.
  - The CSP is `default-src 'none'` with no script source (line 571), which gives defence in depth.
- **Clickjacking:** `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `frame-ancestors 'none'` are sent on HTML responses and redirects (lines 568, 571, 578, 588).
- **Caching and referrer leaks:** `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` are set on every HTML and redirect response (lines 566, 569). Tokens are never placed in URLs.
- **Open redirect and Host header:** `redirect` is only ever called with constant relative paths (`/welcome`, `/login`). The `Host` header and request URLs are never reflected.
- **Rate-limit bypass through headers or paths:**
  - `X-Forwarded-For`-style headers are not trusted, so spoofing them does nothing (line 214).
  - Routing uses an exact `switch` on the path (line 151), so variants such as `/login/` or `/LOGIN` get 404 instead of skipping the limiter.
- **Request parsing:**
  - `Content-Type` must be `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (line 535).
  - The body is capped at 4096 bytes (lines 541-544).
  - Malformed percent-encoding returns 400 (lines 559-560).
  - Duplicate parameters keep the first value (line 557), so there is no parameter pollution.
  - Username and password lengths are bounded (lines 224-226).
- **Error handling:**
  - Unexpected exceptions are logged to stderr, and the client gets a generic message with no stack trace (lines 177-179).
  - `sendErrorIfPossible` avoids writing twice (line 593).
- **HTTP methods:** each route enforces its allowed methods and returns 405 otherwise (lines 153, 157-163, 166, 170, 185-189).
- **Network exposure default:** the server binds to `127.0.0.1` by default (line 83).
- **Categories not present in the code:** no SQL or NoSQL queries, OS command execution, file-system path handling, deserialization, XML parsing, outbound network calls (SSRF), JWTs or third-party dependencies, so injection, XXE, deserialization, SSRF and supply-chain checks do not apply.
- **Non-code files:** `README.md`, `result.md`, `return.txt`, `prompt.txt`, `cyber_prompt.txt` and `prompt_hash.txt` were read. They are documentation, prompts or metadata with no executable content and no secrets.


---

# [74] results-cyber/claude/claude/set_a/sallie/1/security/security_review.md
(finding headings: 7)

# Security Review: SecureLoginServer

## 1. Executive Summary
`SecureLoginServer.java` is a single-file Java 17 web app with no dependencies, built on `com.sun.net.httpserver`. It serves a sign-in form, checks a username and password against PBKDF2-SHA256 hashes kept in memory, and issues a `__Host-SESSIONID` cookie (`Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`). That cookie maps to a session stored on the server. It also serves a home page for signed-in users and a sign-out endpoint protected by a CSRF token. Optional HTTPS uses a PKCS12 keystore.

The core controls are sound: password storage, session ID generation and storage, cookie attributes, session-fixation handling, output encoding and security headers. No injection, XSS, session hijacking or authentication-bypass flaw was found. The findings are about abuse resistance and hardening:

- **Medium:** any unauthenticated client can lock a known username out of sign-in for as long as it likes (SEC-01).
- **Medium:** a handful of slow connections can use up the fixed pool of 16 worker threads, and each login runs a 600,000-iteration PBKDF2 hash (SEC-02).
- **Medium:** the per-IP limit counts every IPv6 address separately, so rotating addresses defeats it (SEC-03).
- **Low:** the lockout check and the failure count are not atomic (SEC-04).
- **Low:** the same-origin check compares `Origin` with the request's own `Host` header and allows requests that send neither header, so it can be passed via DNS rebinding and gives no login-CSRF protection to browsers without `Origin` (SEC-05).
- **Low:** the generated demo password is written to stdout (SEC-06).
- **Low:** a configured password can be as short as one character (SEC-07).

## 2. Scope
| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `SecureLoginServer.java` | The whole application: HTTP/HTTPS server, routing, login, home and logout pages, user store, session store, login throttle, helpers | Password hashing (PBKDF2), `SecureRandom` tokens, session cookie creation and parsing, session timeouts and invalidation, CSRF defences (Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site checks and a synchronizer token), brute-force throttling by username and IP, HTML output encoding, security headers, TLS setup, form parsing and body size limits, logging of usernames and IPs, a secret (the demo password) read from the environment and printed |
| `README.md` | Plain-English guide to running and configuring the app | Documents defaults (loopback bind, HTTPS via keystore), environment variables, a `curl` example and production caveats. No executable code. |
| `prompt.txt`, `cyber_prompt.txt` | The task prompts used to generate the app and this review | None (text only) |
| `result.md`, `return.txt`, `prompt_hash.txt` | Run metadata and summary from the generation step (`prompt_hash.txt` is empty) | None (text/JSON only) |

## 3. Skills Applied
- `review-code-for-security-vulnerabilities`: the router workflow. It was used to understand the code, pick specialised skills by keyword and structure this report.
- `testing-api-authentication-weaknesses`: login flow, account-enumeration resistance, session lifecycle (fixation, logout revocation, expiry), token entropy, tokens in URLs or logs, and password policy (SEC-01, SEC-07).
- `implementing-api-rate-limiting-and-throttling`: `LoginThrottle` and how it is used in `login()`. Checked atomic check-and-increment, client identification, X-Forwarded-For trust and resource exhaustion (SEC-02, SEC-03, SEC-04).
- `performing-csrf-attack-simulation`: `verifySameOrigin()`, the logout CSRF token, SameSite settings and login CSRF (SEC-05).
- `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`: PBKDF2 parameters, salt, constant-time comparison, `SecureRandom` usage, SHA-256 session-ID indexing, TLS protocol versions and keystore secret handling (no finding).
- `performing-security-headers-audit`: CSP, X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Cache-Control, HSTS and cookie attributes (no finding; one hardening note in section 6).
- `testing-for-sensitive-data-exposure`: logging of credentials, error-message leakage, caching of authenticated pages and credentials in URLs (SEC-06).
- `testing-for-xss-vulnerabilities`: every place untrusted data reaches HTML (HTML body and attribute contexts) and the CSP (no finding).
- General OWASP Top 10 / CWE knowledge, used where no library skill closely matched:
  - thread-pool and slow-request exhaustion in the JDK HTTP server (CWE-400)
  - trusting the `Host` header and DNS rebinding against a server bound to loopback (CWE-346)
  - overly restrictive account lockout (CWE-645)
  - log injection (CWE-117)
  - open redirect (CWE-601)
  - HTTP response splitting (CWE-113)
  - path traversal, deserialization and command/SQL injection (confirmed absent)

## 4. Summary of Findings
| ID | Title | Severity | CWE | Location |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SEC-01 | Any client can lock a user out by sending five wrong passwords for that username | Medium | CWE-645 | `SecureLoginServer.java:235` |
| SEC-02 | A few slow connections and costly unauthenticated hashing can use up the 16-thread worker pool | Medium | CWE-400 | `SecureLoginServer.java:122` |
| SEC-03 | Per-IP login limit is keyed on the full IPv6 address, so rotating addresses bypasses it | Medium | CWE-307 | `SecureLoginServer.java:226` |
| SEC-04 | Lockout check and failure recording are not atomic, so parallel guesses exceed the limit | Low | CWE-367 | `SecureLoginServer.java:235` |
| SEC-05 | Same-origin check trusts the request's own Host header and passes when Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site are absent | Low | CWE-346 | `SecureLoginServer.java:327` |
| SEC-06 | Generated demo password is written to stdout/log output | Low | CWE-532 | `SecureLoginServer.java:146` |
| SEC-07 | No minimum strength for the configured account password | Low | CWE-521 | `SecureLoginServer.java:110` |

## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: Any client can lock a user out by sending five wrong passwords for that username
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-645: Overly Restrictive Account Lockout Mechanism
- **Location:** `SecureLoginServer.java:235-237`, `SecureLoginServer.java:534-536` (limit defined at line 73)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// SecureLoginServer.java:235-237
            if (throttle.isLocked(userKey) || throttle.isLocked(ipKey)) {
                sendLoginPage(ex, 429, "Too many failed attempts. Please wait a few minutes and try again.");
                return;
// SecureLoginServer.java:534-536
                if (failures >= maxFailures) {
                    return new Entry(0, now.plus(LOCKOUT_DURATION), now);
                }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The per-user lock applies to the username everywhere, no matter who caused the failures. Once `user:alice` is locked, the check runs before the password is verified, so the real owner gets `429` even with the correct password. Anyone who can reach `/login` can send five wrong passwords for `alice` every five minutes and keep the account locked forever. That costs 5 requests per 5 minutes, and each attempt adds only 1 to the attacker's per-IP counter (limit 20). A single IPv4 address can therefore keep four accounts locked indefinitely, and IPv6 rotation (SEC-03) removes even that limit. Usernames are easy to guess (the default is `alice`), so this is a practical denial of service against sign-in.

**Fix:** Apply the hard lock to the pair of username and client, so an attacker only locks themselves out. Keep a per-username counter with a much higher threshold to stop distributed guessing. Let that username-wide lock be bypassed only by clients the account has already trusted, for example a signed "device cookie" issued after a successful login (OWASP device-cookie pattern).
```java
static final int MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_USER_AND_CLIENT = 5;
static final int MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_USER_GLOBAL = 50;

// in login()
String userKey = "user:" + username;
String pairKey = "user+client:" + username + "|" + ipKey;

if (throttle.isLocked(pairKey) || throttle.isLocked(ipKey)) {
    sendLoginPage(ex, 429, "Too many failed attempts. Please wait a few minutes and try again.");
    return;
}
// A username-wide lock only stops clients the account has never successfully used.
if (throttle.isLocked(userKey) && !hasValidDeviceCookie(ex, username)) {
    sendLoginPage(ex, 429, "Too many failed attempts. Please wait a few minutes and try again.");
    return;
}
...
if (!valid) {
    throttle.recordFailure(pairKey, MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_USER_AND_CLIENT);
    throttle.recordFailure(userKey, MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_USER_GLOBAL);
    throttle.recordFailure(ipKey, MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_IP);
    ...
}
throttle.reset(pairKey);
throttle.reset(userKey);
issueDeviceCookie(ex, username); // HMAC-signed, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict
```

### SEC-02: A few slow connections and costly unauthenticated hashing can use up the 16-thread worker pool
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
- **Location:** `SecureLoginServer.java:84-85`, `SecureLoginServer.java:122-123` (hash cost at line 396)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// SecureLoginServer.java:84-85
        setDefaultProperty("sun.net.httpserver.maxReqTime", "30");
        setDefaultProperty("sun.net.httpserver.maxRspTime", "30");
// SecureLoginServer.java:122-123
        ExecutorService workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
        server.setExecutor(workers);
```

**Why it is a problem:** The JDK `HttpServer` reads each request's line, headers and body (and, for `HttpsServer`, runs the TLS handshake) on the executor thread. Only 16 threads exist, and a request may take up to 30 seconds to arrive. An attacker who opens 16 connections and sends bytes slowly, reopening them every ~30 seconds, holds every worker. Other requests then sit in the executor's unbounded queue, and the site, including sign-in, stops responding. Separately, every unauthenticated `POST /login` with a well-formed body runs PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations (line 396), which uses roughly a CPU core for a noticeable fraction of a second. The throttles only kick in after failures, and SEC-03 lets an attacker avoid the per-IP throttle entirely. Sustained login attempts can therefore saturate the CPU and the pool. Nothing limits concurrent connections or concurrent hashes.

**Fix:** Stop slow clients from pinning scarce platform threads by using virtual threads on Java 21+ or a much larger bounded pool behind a reverse proxy with slow-request protection. Shorten the request timeout, and cap concurrent PBKDF2 work with a semaphore that fails fast with `503`.
```java
setDefaultProperty("sun.net.httpserver.maxReqTime", "10");
setDefaultProperty("sun.net.httpserver.maxRspTime", "10");

// Java 21+: a blocked slow client costs a cheap virtual thread, not one of 16 workers.
ExecutorService workers = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
server.setExecutor(workers);

// Bound CPU spent on unauthenticated password hashing.
static final Semaphore HASH_PERMITS =
        new Semaphore(Math.max(2, Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() / 2));

// in login(), around users.verify(...)
boolean acquired;
try {
    acquired = HASH_PERMITS.tryAcquire(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    acquired = false;
}
if (!acquired) {
    sendLoginPage(ex, 503, "The server is busy. Please try again shortly.");
    return;
}
char[] passwordChars = password.toCharArray();
boolean valid;
try {
    valid = users.verify(username, passwordChars);
} finally {
    Arrays.fill(passwordChars, '\0');
    HASH_PERMITS.release();
}
```

### SEC-03: Per-IP login limit is keyed on the full IPv6 address, so rotating addresses bypasses it
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
- **Location:** `SecureLoginServer.java:226-228`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// SecureLoginServer.java:226-228
            String clientIp = ex.getRemoteAddress().getAddress().getHostAddress();
            String userKey = "user:" + username;
            String ipKey = "ip:" + clientIp;
```

**Why it is a problem:** The per-IP counter uses the full textual address. On an IPv6-reachable deployment (for example, binding to `::` with HTTPS), a single attacker usually controls at least a /64, which is 2^64 source addresses. Using a new address for each attempt means `ip:` never reaches 20 failures. That removes the only control against password spraying (one or two guesses against many usernames) and against the lockout abuse in SEC-01. It also removes the per-client limit on how many PBKDF2 hashes a client can trigger (SEC-02). Each new address also adds an entry to the throttle map.

**Fix:** Group IPv6 clients by their /64 prefix (IPv4 stays per address). Optionally add a global failed-login budget that triggers extra friction such as a CAPTCHA or delay when exceeded.
```java
static String clientKey(InetAddress address) {
    if (address instanceof Inet6Address) {
        // An end site normally owns a whole /64, so count the prefix as one client.
        return "ip6:" + HexFormat.of().formatHex(address.getAddress(), 0, 8);
    }
    return "ip4:" + address.getHostAddress();
}

// in login()
InetAddress clientAddress = ex.getRemoteAddress().getAddress();
String clientIp = clientAddress.getHostAddress();
String userKey = "user:" + username;
String ipKey = clientKey(clientAddress);
```

### SEC-04: Lockout check and failure recording are not atomic, so parallel guesses exceed the limit
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-367: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition
- **Location:** `SecureLoginServer.java:235-250`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// SecureLoginServer.java:235-250
            if (throttle.isLocked(userKey) || throttle.isLocked(ipKey)) {
                sendLoginPage(ex, 429, "Too many failed attempts. Please wait a few minutes and try again.");
                return;
            }

            char[] passwordChars = password.toCharArray();
            boolean valid;
            try {
                valid = users.verify(username, passwordChars);
            } finally {
                Arrays.fill(passwordChars, '\0');
            }

            if (!valid) {
                throttle.recordFailure(userKey, MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_USER);
                throttle.recordFailure(ipKey, MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_IP);
```

**Why it is a problem:** The lock is checked, then a slow PBKDF2 verification runs, and only afterwards is the failure recorded. Requests arriving in parallel all pass `isLocked()` before any of them records a failure. With 16 workers, an attacker can fit up to about 15 extra guesses into each lockout window, roughly four times the documented limit of 5 per user. The per-IP limit is weakened the same way. The rate-limiting skill specifically calls for an atomic check-and-increment.

**Fix:** Reserve the attempt atomically before hashing (inside `ConcurrentHashMap.compute`) and clear the per-user counter on success.
```java
/** Atomically counts an attempt; returns false if the key is already locked. */
boolean tryAcquire(String key, int maxAttempts) {
    Instant now = Instant.now();
    boolean[] allowed = {false};
    entries.compute(key, (k, old) -> {
        if (old != null && old.lockedUntil().isAfter(now)) {
            return old;
        }
        int attempts = old == null || old.lastFailure().isBefore(now.minus(LOCKOUT_DURATION))
                ? 1 : old.failures() + 1;
        allowed[0] = true;
        return attempts >= maxAttempts
                ? new Entry(0, now.plus(LOCKOUT_DURATION), now)
                : new Entry(attempts, Instant.EPOCH, now);
    });
    return allowed[0];
}

// in login(): count the attempt before hashing
if (!throttle.tryAcquire(userKey, MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_USER)
        || !throttle.tryAcquire(ipKey, MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS_PER_IP)) {
    sendLoginPage(ex, 429, "Too many failed attempts. Please wait a few minutes and try again.");
    return;
}
... verify ...
if (valid) {
    throttle.reset(userKey);
}
```

### SEC-05: Same-origin check trusts the request's own Host header and passes when Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site are absent
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-346: Origin Validation Error
- **Location:** `SecureLoginServer.java:327-341`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// SecureLoginServer.java:327-341
        private void verifySameOrigin(HttpExchange ex) {
            Headers h = ex.getRequestHeaders();
            String fetchSite = h.getFirst("Sec-Fetch-Site");
            if (fetchSite != null && !fetchSite.equals("same-origin") && !fetchSite.equals("none")) {
                throw new HttpError(403, "Cross-site request rejected.");
            }
            String origin = h.getFirst("Origin");
            if (origin != null) {
                String host = h.getFirst("Host");
                String expected = (https ? "https://" : "http://") + host;
                if (host == null || !origin.equalsIgnoreCase(expected)) {
                    throw new HttpError(403, "Cross-site request rejected.");
                }
            }
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:** There are two weaknesses.

1. **The expected origin comes from the request's own `Host` header.** The check therefore only confirms `Origin == Host`, not that the request is for this application's real origin, and no Host allow-list exists anywhere. In the default plain-HTTP mode the server listens on `127.0.0.1:8080`. A malicious website can use DNS rebinding to point `evil.example` at `127.0.0.1`. The victim's browser then sends `Origin: http://evil.example:8080` with `Host: evil.example:8080`, which passes the check, and the attacker's script can read the responses. From the victim's machine it can:
   - guess passwords (the responses act as an oracle);
   - lock the local account (SEC-01);
   - use up the shared `127.0.0.1` per-IP budget, which blocks every local user.
2. **The check allows requests that carry neither `Sec-Fetch-Site` nor `Origin`.** The login form has no CSRF token, so login CSRF protection depends entirely on these headers. Browsers that omit them get no protection.

HTTPS mode limits the first issue, because rebinding breaks certificate name validation.

**Fix:** Validate `Host` against a configured allow-list on every request. Compare `Origin` with the configured public origin, and reject state-changing requests that carry neither header. Command-line clients such as the README's `curl` example then need `-H 'Origin: http://localhost:8080'`.
```java
// configured once, e.g. from APP_PUBLIC_ORIGIN (default "http://localhost:" + port)
private final String publicOrigin;
private final Set<String> allowedHosts; // e.g. Set.of("localhost:8080", "127.0.0.1:8080")

// at the start of handle(), before routing
String host = ex.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Host");
if (host == null || !allowedHosts.contains(host.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT))) {
    throw new HttpError(400, "Unknown host.");
}

private void verifySameOrigin(HttpExchange ex) {
    Headers h = ex.getRequestHeaders();
    String fetchSite = h.getFirst("Sec-Fetch-Site");
    if (fetchSite != null && !fetchSite.equals("same-origin") && !fetchSite.equals("none")) {
        throw new HttpError(403, "Cross-site request rejected.");
    }
    String origin = h.getFirst("Origin");
    if (origin == null && fetchSite == null) {
        // Fail closed: without either header the request's origin cannot be established.
        throw new HttpError(403, "Cross-site request rejected.");
    }
    if (origin != null && !origin.equalsIgnoreCase(publicOrigin)) {
        throw new HttpError(403, "Cross-site request rejected.");
    }
}
```

### SEC-06: Generated demo password is written to stdout/log output
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
- **Location:** `SecureLoginServer.java:146-148`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// SecureLoginServer.java:146-148
        if (generatedPassword) {
            log("No APP_DEMO_PASSWORD set. Demo account -> username: " + demoUsername
                    + "  password: " + demoPassword);
```

**Why it is a problem:** When `APP_DEMO_PASSWORD` is not set, the working password is printed through the normal `log()` channel on stdout. When the app runs under systemd, Docker, Kubernetes or a CI runner, stdout is captured and kept by log collectors that are often readable by many more people than the host. Anyone with log access can then sign in. The README warns against doing this "with real accounts", but the code does it by default without checking where stdout goes.

**Fix:** Don't send the secret through the logging channel. Show it only on an interactive terminal, and otherwise require the operator to set `APP_DEMO_PASSWORD`. On JDK 22+ also check `Console.isTerminal()`, because `System.console()` may return a non-null console when output is redirected.
```java
if (generatedPassword) {
    java.io.Console console = System.console();
    if (console != null) {
        // Shown once on the interactive terminal only; never written through log().
        console.printf("Demo account -> username: %s  password: %s%n", demoUsername, demoPassword);
    } else {
        fail("No interactive terminal: set APP_DEMO_PASSWORD instead of relying on a generated password.");
    }
} else {
    log("Demo account '" + demoUsername + "' loaded from environment.");
}
```

### SEC-07: No minimum strength for the configured account password
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-521: Weak Password Requirements
- **Location:** `SecureLoginServer.java:105-113`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// SecureLoginServer.java:105-113
        String demoPassword = System.getenv("APP_DEMO_PASSWORD");
        boolean generatedPassword = demoPassword == null || demoPassword.isEmpty();
        if (generatedPassword) {
            demoPassword = randomToken().substring(0, 20);
        }
        if (demoUsername.isEmpty() || demoUsername.length() > MAX_USERNAME_LENGTH
                || demoPassword.length() > MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) {
            fail("Demo username or password has an invalid length.");
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:** Only a maximum length is enforced. `APP_DEMO_PASSWORD=a` or `APP_DEMO_PASSWORD=password` is accepted and becomes the account's password. Combined with the default username `alice` and the throttle weaknesses above (SEC-03, SEC-04), a weak password can be guessed within a few lockout windows. `addUser()` is the template for loading real users, and it has no policy hook either.

**Fix:** Enforce a minimum length (NIST SP 800-63B recommends at least 15 characters for single-factor passwords) and reject known-common passwords before hashing.
```java
static final int MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH = 15;

String demoPassword = System.getenv("APP_DEMO_PASSWORD");
boolean generatedPassword = demoPassword == null || demoPassword.isEmpty();
if (generatedPassword) {
    demoPassword = randomToken().substring(0, 20);
}
if (demoUsername.isEmpty() || demoUsername.length() > MAX_USERNAME_LENGTH
        || demoPassword.length() < MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH
        || demoPassword.length() > MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH
        || CommonPasswords.contains(demoPassword)) {
    fail("Demo username or password is invalid: the password needs at least "
            + MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH + " characters and must not be a common password.");
}
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding
- **Password storage:** PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 with 600,000 iterations, a 16-byte per-user salt from `SecureRandom` and a 256-bit output (lines 395-398, 425-440). This meets OWASP 2023 guidance. The password spec is cleared after use (line 438), and password char arrays are wiped (lines 245, 412).
- **Constant-time comparison:** the password hash (line 420) and the CSRF token (lines 297, 675-677) are compared with `MessageDigest.isEqual`.
- **Account enumeration:** unknown usernames are hashed against a dummy credential, so timing matches real accounts (lines 404-406, 416-423). Wrong username and wrong password both give the same `401` message (line 254). The lockout response does not reveal whether an account exists.
- **Session ID entropy and storage:** 256-bit `SecureRandom` tokens encoded as Base64URL (lines 680-684). IDs are stored only as SHA-256 hashes (lines 471-476), and incoming values must match a strict format before lookup (lines 79, 479, 497).
- **Session fixation:** any existing session is invalidated and a new ID issued on successful login (lines 264-266).
- **Session expiry and revocation:** 15-minute idle and 8-hour absolute timeouts are enforced on every lookup (lines 458-460, 488-491). Logout removes the server-side session and expires the cookie (lines 300-303). A background job purges expired sessions (lines 131-134).
- **Cookie attributes:** `__Host-` prefix, `Path=/`, `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, no `Domain`, and no persistent expiry (lines 67, 365-372). The session value holds no user data. Cookie parsing matches the exact name (lines 374-389).
- **CSRF on authenticated actions:** logout requires POST (line 194), a per-session 256-bit token checked in constant time (lines 285, 296-299) and the Sec-Fetch-Site/Origin checks. `SameSite=Strict` stops the cookie being sent cross-site. Login CSRF residual risk is covered in SEC-05.
- **XSS / output encoding:** every dynamic value put into HTML goes through `escapeHtml`, which encodes `& < > " '` (lines 660-673). This covers:
  - error messages (line 203)
  - the username and timestamp (lines 281-282)
  - the CSRF token in an attribute (line 285)
  - login errors (line 307)
  - page titles (lines 656-657)

  No input is reflected without encoding. The CSP `default-src 'none'` blocks all script (lines 346-347).
- **Security headers:** CSP with `frame-ancestors 'none'`, `form-action 'self'` and `base-uri 'none'`, plus `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and `Cache-Control: no-store` on every response (lines 343-351).
