## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01 — Client IP spoofed via leftmost `X-Forwarded-For`

- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-290 (Authentication Bypass by Spoofing) / CWE-346 (Origin Validation Error) / CWE-348 (Use of Less Trusted Source)
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/HttpRequestContext.java:42`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
                if (config.isTrustForwardedHeaders()) {
                    String forwarded = request.getHeader(config.getTrustedProxyIpHeader());
                    if (forwarded != null && !forwarded.isBlank()) {
                        // Take the leftmost IP from forwarded header and sanitize
                        String firstIp = forwarded.split(",")[0].trim();
                        if (isValidIp(firstIp)) {
                            return firstIp;
                        }
                    }
                }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
`getRemoteAddr()` returns the leftmost entry of a request header the caller fully controls, and that value is used as `remoteIp` throughout `PostAuthSessionCookieHandler` — as the key for `rateLimiter.tryAcquire(remoteIp, userId)` / `recordOutcome(...)` (the IP and IP+account throttle buckets) and in every `logger.warn(... ip=... )` audit line. When `trustForwardedHeaders` is enabled there is no check that the socket peer is actually a trusted proxy, so any client can set `X-Forwarded-For: <random>` on every request. Each request then hashes to a fresh IP bucket, so the 20-req/min IP limit and the 10/min IP+account limit are trivially bypassed — reducing the dual-key limiter to the global account limit only and enabling distributed credential stuffing / brute force. The same forgery poisons the audit trail so incident response attributes abuse to innocent addresses. The leftmost position is also the *least* trustworthy hop: standard practice is that the leftmost value is attacker-chosen while only the hop appended by the last trusted proxy is authoritative. The weak `isValidIp` format check (allows any `[0-9a-fA-F.:]` up to 45 chars, no octet-range or IPv6 validation) does not constrain this — any of `1.2.3.4`, `dead::beef`, or `999.999.999.999` is accepted as a distinct key.

**Fix:**
Only consult forwarded headers when the direct socket peer is itself a trusted proxy, and derive the client IP from the rightmost hop appended by trusted infrastructure (or the standard `Forwarded` header), never the caller-supplied leftmost value.

```java
// Config must declare the trusted proxy CIDRs; a single boolean is not enough.
@Override
public String getRemoteAddr() {
    String socketAddr = request.getRemoteAddr();
    if (socketAddr == null || socketAddr.isBlank()) {
        return "0.0.0.0";
    }
    // Only parse forwarded headers if the immediate peer is a known proxy.
    if (config.isTrustForwardedHeaders() && config.isTrustedProxy(socketAddr)) {
        String forwarded = request.getHeader(config.getTrustedProxyIpHeader());
        if (forwarded != null && !forwarded.isBlank()) {
            String[] hops = forwarded.split(",");
            // Walk right-to-left, returning the first hop NOT in the trusted set;
            // that hop was appended by the last trusted proxy and is authoritative.
            for (int i = hops.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
                String hop = hops[i].trim();
                if (isValidIp(hop) && !config.isTrustedProxy(hop)) {
                    return hop;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return socketAddr; // fall back to the authenticated socket address
}
```
Additionally, harden `isValidIp` to real IPv4/IPv6 parsing (e.g. `InetAddress` with literal-only checks, or `InetAddresses.isInetAddress`) so malformed values cannot mint arbitrary bucket keys.

### SEC-02 — TLS gate satisfied by attacker-controlled `X-Forwarded-Proto`

- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-319 (Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information) / CWE-290 (Authentication Bypass by Spoofing)
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/HttpRequestContext.java:61`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
                if (request.isSecure()) {
                    return true;
                }
                if (config.isTrustForwardedHeaders()) {
                    String proto = request.getHeader("X-Forwarded-Proto");
                    if ("https".equalsIgnoreCase(proto)) {
                        return true;
                    }
                }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
`isSecure()` returns `true` when the header `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` is present, regardless of the actual transport. The handler's mandatory TLS gate at `PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:132` (`if (config.isRequireSecureTransport() && !request.isSecure())`) relies on this, and its pass-through is what lets the handler emit a session cookie with the `Secure` flag and a `__Host-` prefix. If the component is ever reachable over plain HTTP and `trustForwardedHeaders` is enabled, an attacker (or a network interceptor on a downgraded connection) simply adds `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, defeats the "insecure transport rejected" control, and a session cookie is set on a plaintext channel — where it is sniffable. The value here is a header the client controls, so it is not evidence of transport security; it is only trustworthy if injected by a TLS-terminating proxy that also strips any client-supplied copy.

**Fix:**
Do not derive transport security from a client-influenceable header. Rely on the container's own `request.isSecure()` (or an explicitly configured TLS port), and only accept a forwarded-protocol hint after confirming the socket peer is a trusted proxy that overwrites (not appends to) the header:

```java
@Override
public boolean isSecure() {
    if (request.isSecure()) {
        return true; // authoritative: TLS at the servlet container
    }
    // Never trust X-Forwarded-Proto from an unverified peer.
    if (config.isTrustForwardedHeaders()
            && config.isTrustedProxy(request.getRemoteAddr())) {
        // A trusted, TLS-terminating proxy must set this authoritatively;
        // require an exact match and assume it strips client-supplied copies.
        return "https".equals(request.getHeader("X-Forwarded-Proto"));
    }
    return false;
}
```
Pair this with HSTS at the edge and configure the reverse proxy to remove inbound `X-Forwarded-Proto` before setting it.

### SEC-03 — Per-IP failure penalty never expires; throttle path never records an outcome → permanent IP lockout

- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption) / CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling)
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/DualKeyBoundedRateLimiter.java:104` (related: `DualKeyBoundedRateLimiter.java:66`, `DualKeyBoundedRateLimiter.java:175`; `src/main/java/com/security/session/PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:141`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
        void resetIfExpired(long nowMs, long windowMillis) {
            if (nowMs - windowStartMs >= windowMillis) {
                windowStartMs = nowMs;
                count = 0;
            }
            lastAccessMs = nowMs;
        }
```
```java
            if (counter.consecutiveFailures >= ipMaxConsecutiveFailures) {
                long retryAfter = Math.max(1, (windowMillis - (now - counter.windowStartMs)) / 1000);
                ipResult[0] = new EvaluationResult(false, "IP blocked due to excessive failures", retryAfter);
                return counter;
            }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The class Javadoc and the handler comment ("penalizes abusive IP without locking out legitimate user") state that per-IP penalties must be self-healing. They are not. `resetIfExpired()` zeroes `count` on window expiry but **never touches `consecutiveFailures`** (the field is only reset in the constructor at line 62 and by a *successful* `recordOutcome`). `consecutiveFailures` is incremented on every failed validation and only cleared to 0 on a successful post-auth from that exact IP. Consequently, once an IP accrues `ipMaxConsecutiveFailures` (default 5) failures, `tryAcquire` returns `blocked` at line 104 — and because the throttle branch in the handler (`PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:141`–`149`) returns 429 **without calling `recordOutcome`**, there is no path that ever resets the counter except a future success from the same IP, which the block now prevents. The IP is permanently locked out until its bucket is evicted from memory (`lastAccessMs` idle for 2×window). This is a persistent denial of service for every user behind a shared/NAT egress, corporate proxy, or mobile carrier after a handful of mistyped sessions or one burst of attacker traffic aimed at a victim's shared IP — and the attacker can *seed* it cheaply, since 5 failures suffice. `Retry-After` is also misreported (computed from the count window, not the penalty), giving false guidance.

**Fix:**
Age the penalty independently of the request-count window: store a `penaltyUntilMs` (or decay `consecutiveFailures` on a longer penalty window) so a blocked IP becomes eligible again, and clear it via a dedicated expiry rather than only via success.

```java
static final class WindowCounter {
    long windowStartMs;
    int count;
    int consecutiveFailures;
    long penaltyUntilMs;     // NEW: independent, expiring penalty deadline
    long lastAccessMs;

    void resetIfExpired(long nowMs, long windowMillis) {
        if (nowMs - windowStartMs >= windowMillis) {
            windowStartMs = nowMs;
            count = 0;
        }
        lastAccessMs = nowMs;
    }
}

// In tryAcquire, replace the >= ipMaxConsecutiveFailures check with:
if (counter.penaltyUntilMs > now) {
    long retryAfter = Math.max(1, (counter.penaltyUntilMs - now) / 1000);
    ipResult[0] = new EvaluationResult(false, "IP temporarily blocked due to excessive failures", retryAfter);
    return counter;
}

// In recordOutcome, on failure set an expiring penalty instead of a sticky counter:
} else {
    counter.consecutiveFailures++;
    if (counter.consecutiveFailures >= ipMaxConsecutiveFailures) {
        counter.penaltyUntilMs = now + penaltyWindowMillis; // e.g. 5–15 min, self-expiring
    }
}
```

### SEC-04 — Capacity eviction removes arbitrary in-window buckets

- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-695 (Use of Off-the-Shelf Cryptography with Errors) → more precisely CWE-307 (Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts) via control-bypass
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/DualKeyBoundedRateLimiter.java:218`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
    private void evictIfOverCapacity(ConcurrentHashMap<String, WindowCounter> map) {
        if (map.size() <= maxEntries) {
            return;
        }
        // Remove oldest entries until under threshold
        int toRemove = map.size() - maxEntries;
        Iterator<String> iterator = map.keySet().iterator();
        while (iterator.hasNext() && toRemove > 0) {
            iterator.next();
            iterator.remove();
            toRemove--;
        }
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The comment claims it removes "the oldest entries," but `ConcurrentHashMap.keySet().iterator()` has no age ordering — it walks the hash table in arbitrary slot order. The eviction therefore discards essentially random buckets, including freshly-populated ones that are actively throttling an abuser. An attacker who can drive the maps toward `maxEntries` (default 10,000 distinct IP / IP+account / account keys — cheap to generate by rotating a spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` per SEC-01, or distinct `userId` strings) can force repeated `ensureCapacity()`/`evictIfOverCapacity()` cycles that evict their own in-progress counters, resetting their rate-limit state mid-attack and nullifying the brute-force protection. It also drops the failure-penalty state that SEC-03 depends on. This turns the memory bound into a throttle-defeating lever.

**Fix:**
Evict by staleness using the `lastAccessMs` the counter already tracks (LRU), not hash order, so recently-seen buckets that carry live rate-limit state survive:

```java
    private void evictIfOverCapacity(ConcurrentHashMap<String, WindowCounter> map) {
        if (map.size() <= maxEntries) {
            return;
        }
        int toRemove = map.size() - maxEntries;
        // Evict the least-recently-accessed entries (true LRU) by lastAccessMs.
        List<Map.Entry<String, WindowCounter>> entries = new ArrayList<>(map.entrySet());
        entries.sort(Comparator.comparingLong(e -> e.getValue().lastAccessMs));
        Iterator<Map.Entry<String, WindowCounter>> it = entries.iterator();
        while (it.hasNext() && toRemove > 0) {
            Map.Entry<String, WindowCounter> e = it.next();
            map.remove(e.getKey(), e.getValue()); // CAS-remove: only if unchanged
            toRemove--;
        }
    }
```

### SEC-05 — Fixed-window counters allow ~2× burst at the window boundary

- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-307 (Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts)
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/DualKeyBoundedRateLimiter.java:66`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
        void resetIfExpired(long nowMs, long windowMillis) {
            if (nowMs - windowStartMs >= windowMillis) {
                windowStartMs = nowMs;
                count = 0;
            }
            lastAccessMs = nowMs;
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
This is a classic fixed-window counter: on expiry the window start is moved to `now` and the count is hard-reset to 0 with no memory of the prior window's tail. An attacker can spend the full `ipLimit` (20) requests in the last instant of one window and the full 20 again in the first instant of the next, achieving ~40 requests in a short real-time span — roughly double the intended sustained rate for a burst. The same applies to the IP+account (10) and global account (60) buckets. For a session-issuance endpoint this materially raises the number of guesses a rate limiter will tolerate per wall-clock second during a credential-stuffing or session-ID-guessing attempt. It is a real weakening of the throttle, though bounded by the ceiling (not unbounded), hence Medium rather than High.

**Fix:**
Replace the hard reset with a sliding window (weighted by elapsed time into the previous window) or a token bucket, so the limit reflects the trailing `windowMillis` of real time rather than an arbitrary calendar boundary:

```java
        long windowStartMs;
        int count;             // current window
        int prevCount;         // previous window (for sliding weighted estimate)

        void resetIfExpired(long nowMs, long windowMillis) {
            long elapsed = nowMs - windowStartMs;
            if (elapsed >= windowMillis * 2) {          // fully aged out
                prevCount = 0;
                count = 0;
                windowStartMs = nowMs;
            } else if (elapsed >= windowMillis) {        // roll to a new window
                prevCount = count;
                count = 0;
                windowStartMs += windowMillis;
            }
            lastAccessMs = nowMs;
        }

        // Effective estimate used by tryAcquire instead of raw count:
        double slidingEstimate(long nowMs, long windowMillis) {
            double weight = 1.0 - ((nowMs - windowStartMs) / (double) windowMillis);
            return count + prevCount * weight;
        }
```
(`tryAcquire` then compares `slidingEstimate(...) >= ipLimit` instead of `count >= ipLimit`.)

### SEC-06 — Differentiated status codes and success-path timing gap leave an enumeration/timing oracle

- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-208 (Observable Discrepancy)
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:132` (related: `PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:154`, `PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:254`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
        if (config.isRequireSecureTransport() && !request.isSecure()) {
            performConstantTimeDummyWork();
            logger.warn("Insecure transport rejected for session cookie: ip={}, user={}",
                    remoteIp, sanitizeForLog(userId));
            return failClosed(response, 400, "INSECURE_TRANSPORT", "Session cookie cannot be issued over insecure transport");
        }
```
```java
        private void performConstantTimeDummyWork() {
            try {
                MessageDigest digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
                digest.update(DUMMY_SALT);
                digest.digest();
            } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException ignored) {
            }
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The code deliberately runs `performConstantTimeDummyWork()` on the failure branches (insecure transport, throttle, session-claim failure, cookie-build failure) to equalize timing, which shows the authors were aware of the risk — but the mitigation is incomplete and the observable surface is not just timing. The failure paths return distinct HTTP status codes (400 for validation/transport, 401 for session-claim failure, 429 for throttle, 500 for cookie-build error) and distinct `errorCode` values surfaced in `PostAuthResult`, and the session-claim path (line 154) reaches `validateAndClaimSession` which itself returns distinguishable results (`SESSION_NOT_FOUND` vs `ALREADY_CLAIMED` vs `USER_MISMATCH`, `InMemorySessionStateValidator.java:84`–`108`). An attacker probing `userId`/`sessionId` pairs can thus distinguish "session exists but wrong user" from "session not found" from "already claimed" purely from status/behavior, enabling account and session-identifier enumeration. The dummy work also runs only on failure — the *success* path performs strictly more work (cookie build + `recordOutcome(true)`), so overall latency still separates success from failure, meaning the single-SHA dummy does not actually flatten the distribution it is meant to hide. The generic JSON bodies (`GENERIC_*`) are good for the response body, but the status codes and the distinguishable validator results re-introduce the oracle.

**Fix:**
Return a single uniform client status and body for all "invalid credential/session" outcomes, and run a *balanced* amount of work on every path (including success) — ideally a fixed total budget rather than a lone SHA. Keep granular reasons in the internal audit log only.

```java
// Collapse all authentication/session failures into one indistinguishable 401:
SessionValidationResult sessionResult = sessionValidator.validateAndClaimSession(sessionId, userId);
performConstantTimeDummyWork(); // run on BOTH success and failure, not only failure
if (!sessionResult.isSuccess()) {
    rateLimiter.recordOutcome(remoteIp, userId, false);
    logger.warn("Session claim failed: code={}, ip={}, user={}, token={}",
            sessionResult.getErrorCode(), remoteIp, sanitizeForLog(userId),
            CookieSecurityUtil.maskToken(sessionId));
    // Same status + same body for not-found / revoked / expired / mismatch / already-claimed.
    return failClosed(response, 401, "AUTHENTICATION_FAILED", "Invalid session or credentials");
}
// ...success continues with the identical status/body shape.
```
For timing, replace the single `digest.digest()` with a fixed-iteration budget executed unconditionally (or enforce a minimum per-request latency floor), so success and failure cannot be separated by response time.

### SEC-07 — Session secret copied from `char[]` into an immutable `String` before zeroisation

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-316 (Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information in Memory)
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:91`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
        try {
            String sessionId = (sessionIdChars != null) ? new String(sessionIdChars) : null;
            return handlePostAuthentication(request, response, sessionId, userId);
        } finally {
            if (sessionIdChars != null) {
                Arrays.fill(sessionIdChars, '\0');
            }
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The `char[]` overload is clearly designed to keep the session secret in a zeroisable buffer — the `finally` block scrubs it. But line 91 immediately copies the secret into an immutable `java.lang.String`. That `String` lives on the heap until garbage collection, cannot be proactively cleared (interning/immutability), and may also be copied again during concatenation inside `buildSetCookieHeader` and the masking path. The `Arrays.fill` on the `char[]` therefore gives a false sense of hygiene: the authoritative secret persists in a non-wipeable form, defeating the purpose of accepting `char[]` in the first place. Impact is bounded (a heap-dump/forensic exposure requirement, and session IDs are single-use and short-lived), hence Low, but it silently nullifies an intended control.

**Fix:**
Propagate the secret as `char[]`/`ByteBuffer` through the code path and zeroise at the single point of last use, avoiding immutable `String` copies of the secret. Where the API boundary must accept a `String` (e.g. the validator), minimize the window and prefer arrays internally:

```java
    public PostAuthResult handlePostAuthentication(
            HttpServletRequest request,
            HttpServletResponse response,
            char[] sessionIdChars,
            String userId) throws IOException {

        // Do NOT create an immutable String copy of the secret.
        // Pass the mutable buffer down; buildSetCookieHeader and the validator
        // should accept char[] (or build the header in place) and we zeroise
        // exactly once, in this finally, at the true point of last use.
        try {
            return handlePostAuthentication(request, response, sessionIdChars, userId);
        } finally {
            if (sessionIdChars != null) {
                Arrays.fill(sessionIdChars, '\0');
            }
        }
    }
```
If refactoring the whole chain is out of scope, at minimum document that the secret is retained by the `String` copy and ensure a short GC/retention posture; the correct fix is to keep it in a wipeable buffer end-to-end.

### SEC-08 — Caller-supplied validation regexes compiled and matched without ReDoS safety check

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-1333 (Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity)
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/SessionCookieConfig.java:191` (also `SessionCookieConfig.java:200`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
        public Builder sessionIdConstraints(int minLength, int maxLength, String regexPattern) {
            if (minLength < 16) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Minimum session ID length must be at least 16 characters for security entropy");
            }
            if (maxLength < minLength || maxLength > 512) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Maximum session ID length must be between minLength and 512 characters");
            }
            this.minSessionIdLength = minLength;
            this.maxSessionIdLength = maxLength;
            this.sessionIdPattern = Pattern.compile(regexPattern);
            return this;
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
`sessionIdConstraints(...)` and `userIdConstraints(...)` accept an arbitrary `regexPattern` from the integrating application and compile it verbatim (lines 191 and 200) with no safety inspection; that `Pattern` is then matched against externally supplied `sessionId`/`userId` values on the request path. If a developer supplies a pattern with catastrophic backtracking (nested quantifiers, alternation overlap), an attacker who submits a crafted long near-matching string can trigger exponential match time and a CPU-denial-of-service. This is rated Low because the *shipped defaults* are linear and safe (`^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,128}$` and `^[A-Za-z0-9_.@-]{1,64}$`), and the exploitability depends on an integrator choosing a bad pattern — but the API invites it and applies no guard, and the input is attacker-controlled and length-bounded only to 512 chars (still ample for a catastrophic pattern).

**Fix:**
Validate the supplied pattern against a safe subset (or run matching under a timeout / on a bounded matcher), and reject known-catastrophic shapes before accepting them. A pragmatic, robust option is to enforce matching under a `CharSequence` watchdog or to require a linear-time engine:

```java
    public Builder sessionIdConstraints(int minLength, int maxLength, String regexPattern) {
        // ... existing length checks ...
        this.sessionIdPattern = compileSafe(regexPattern);
        return this;
    }

    private static Pattern compileSafe(String regex) {
        // Reject constructs strongly associated with catastrophic backtracking,
        // e.g. nested quantifiers ((a+)+), overlapping alternations, etc.
        if (UNSAFE_REGEX.matcher(regex).find()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                "Regex contains constructs with potential catastrophic backtracking");
        }
        // Prefer a linear-time engine (e.g. RE2/J) or, with java.util.regex,
        // cap the input to maxSessionIdLength and match with a watchdog timeout.
        return Pattern.compile(regex);
    }
```
At minimum, bound match input to `maxSessionIdLength`/`maxUserIdLength` before matching (already partly done) and document the ReDoS hazard of supplying custom patterns.

### SEC-09 — Session claim not rolled back on later cookie-build failure; `registerSession` silently overwrites

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-664 (Improper Control of a Resource Through its Lifetime) / CWE-367 (Time-of-check Time-of-use Race Condition)
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/session/InMemorySessionStateValidator.java:74` (also `InMemorySessionStateValidator.java:107`; `src/main/java/com/security/session/PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:170`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
        sessions.put(sessionId, new ServerSessionRecord(sessionId, userId, Instant.now(), expiresAt));
    }
```
```java
        // Atomic check-and-act: claim the session once
        if (!record.claimed.compareAndSet(false, true)) {
            return SessionValidationResult.failure("ALREADY_CLAIMED", "Session has already been claimed / issued");
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
Two lifetime-integrity issues. (1) In the handler, `validateAndClaimSession` atomically flips `claimed` to `true` (line 107) *before* `buildSetCookieHeader` runs. If that build throws `SecurityValidationException`, the handler returns 500 (`PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.java:170`–`174`) but the session stays marked `claimed=true` in the store — the claim is never rolled back. Because the record is single-use, the legitimate user's freshly-issued session is now permanently `ALREADY_CLAIMED` and cannot be redeemed, while no cookie was ever delivered: a self-inflicted single-session lockout triggered by any cookie-build error. (2) `registerSession` (line 74) uses an unconditional `sessions.put(...)`, so re-registering an existing `sessionId` blindly replaces the record, silently discarding its `claimed`/`revoked` state — a previously claimed or revoked session would revert to unclaimed, allowing re-issuance. `registerSession` is documented as called by a trusted upstream, which keeps this Low, but it is still a state-loss footgun, and expired records are only swept when capacity is hit or lazily on access.

**Fix:**
Only flip the claim once the cookie header is known to be constructible (claim last, or roll back on failure), and make registration refuse to clobber an existing live record.

```java
// Handler: build the header BEFORE the irreversible single-use claim.
String setCookieHeader;
try {
    setCookieHeader = CookieSecurityUtil.buildSetCookieHeader(config, sessionId);
} catch (SecurityValidationException e) {
    performConstantTimeDummyWork();
    logger.error("Failed to build Set-Cookie header: reason={}", e.getInternalAuditReason());
    return failClosed(response, 500, "COOKIE_BUILD_ERROR", e.getInternalAuditReason());
    // Session NOT yet claimed -> legitimate user can retry.
}
// Claim only now that the response is guaranteed buildable:
SessionValidationResult sessionResult = sessionValidator.validateAndClaimSession(sessionId, userId);
```
```java
// Validator: do not silently overwrite an existing session's lifecycle state.
public void registerSession(String sessionId, String userId, Instant expiresAt) {
    if (sessionId == null || userId == null || expiresAt == null) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Session registration arguments cannot be null");
    }
    // ... capacity handling ...
    sessions.compute(sessionId, (k, existing) -> {
        if (existing != null && !existing.isExpired() ) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Session already registered; refusing to overwrite");
        }
        return new ServerSessionRecord(sessionId, userId, Instant.now(), expiresAt);
    });
}
```
If a rollback-after-claim design is preferred instead, add `releaseClaim(sessionId)` that CAS's `claimed` back to `false` on the cookie-build failure path.

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding

The following controls were examined and are correctly implemented — recorded here to show what was checked, not missed:

- **`HttpOnly` is non-writable.** `SessionCookieConfig` declares `httpOnly` as `final true` with no builder setter, so callers cannot disable it. Correct.
- **`__Host-` / `__Secure-` / `SameSite=None` prefix rules enforced at build time.** `build()` (SessionCookieConfig.java:248+) rejects `__Host-` without `Secure`/`Path=/`/no `Domain`, rejects `__Secure-` without `Secure`, and rejects `SameSite=None` without `Secure`. Cookie name/path/domain are validated against safe regexes. Correct (the residual risk in SEC-02 is transport determination, not the prefix logic).
- **`Secure` default is safe and `Max-Age` is bounded.** Default `secure=true`, `requireSecureTransport=true`, and `Max-Age` is clamped to `[-1, 2_592_000]` (≤30 days), preventing runaway session lifetimes. `Partitioned` (CHIPS) is emitted only when `secure` is set.
- **Response-splitting / cookie-injection defence is present and correct.** `CookieSecurityUtil.assertNoControlCharacters` rejects CR, LF, all `0x00`–`0x1F` and `0x7F`; `assertNoHeaderDelimiters` rejects `;`, `,`, space and tab in the value, applied during `buildSetCookieHeader` on value/path/domain. `PostAuthSessionCookieHandler.sanitizeForLog` also strips `\r\n\t` before logging, preventing log-injection through `userId`.
- **Secrets are masked in every log line.** The raw session ID is never logged; `CookieSecurityUtil.maskToken` emits a `[sha256:xxxxxxxx...]` fingerprint (8-hex prefix), and the client-facing bodies are fixed generic JSON while internal reasons stay in the audit log via the `SecurityValidationResult` client-vs-internal message split.
- **Constant-time comparisons are used where secrets/identity are compared.** `CookieSecurityUtil.constantTimeEquals` and `InMemorySessionStateValidator.validateAndClaimSession` both use `MessageDigest.isEqual`, avoiding byte-position timing leaks on the user-ID comparison (the remaining timing concern in SEC-06 is branch/latency structure, not the equality primitive).
- **Single-use claim is genuinely atomic.** `record.claimed.compareAndSet(false, true)` (with `AtomicBoolean`) correctly serializes concurrent redemption so a session cannot be double-issued. Revocation and expiry are checked before the claim, and expired sessions are removed on access.
- **Rate-limiter maps are memory-bounded and keys are size-capped.** `maxEntries` bounds each of the three buckets, `sanitizeKey` truncates keys to 128 chars, and `purgeExpiredMap` removes entries idle beyond 2×window — the *memory* bound is sound; SEC-03/SEC-04/SEC-05 concern the eviction *selection* and penalty lifecycle, not unbounded growth.
- **Input validation runs before any privileged operation.** `validateInputs` enforces non-null/non-blank, length bounds, whitelist regex, and rejects control characters and cookie delimiters on both `sessionId` and `userId` before TLS/rate-limit/session work, and the handler fails closed (returns an error result) at every rejection point.
- **Cache-prevention headers are correct and applied on both success and failure paths.** `setSecurityHeaders` sets `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private`, `Pragma: no-cache`, `Expires: 0`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and is invoked on the throttle path as well as success.
- **Test doubles are correctly scoped.** `SimpleHttpRequestContext` / `SimpleHttpResponseContext` are `HashMap`-backed and non-thread-safe, but live only under `src/test/` and are not in the production path — no finding.
- **Dependencies introduce no known vulnerable component or secret.** `pom.xml` pins `jakarta.servlet-api` (provided), `slf4j-api`, and JUnit (test), sets `source/target 17` and `-Werror`, and contains no credentials.

# [147] results-cyber/qwen/agy/set_a/post_research/2/security/security_review.md
(finding headings: 9)

# Security Review: Secure Symmetric Crypto Component (com.security.crypto)

## 1. Executive Summary

The component is a dependency-free Java 17 library for AES-256-GCM symmetric encryption at rest: an encrypt/decrypt service with per-message random IVs, an authenticated custom wire format (`SEC1` magic + version + keyId + IV + ciphertext‖tag), pluggable in-memory and PKCS#12 KeyStore key providers with rotation/revocation, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 key derivation, key-file permission hardening, and a dual-bucket decryption-failure rate limiter. Core cryptography is sound: AES-256-GCM with 128-bit tags, `SecureRandom` for all nonces/keys/salts, defensive copies, uniform post-lookup decryption errors, and best-effort key zeroization.

The most important findings are in the **control layer around** the cryptography, not in the primitives:

1. **`encrypt()` reads the active key and its ID in two unsynchronized steps**, so a concurrent `rotateKey()` (documented as "atomic" but implemented as two writes) can produce a ciphertext permanently mislabeled with the wrong keyId — silent, unrecoverable data loss (SEC-01).
2. **Key-file validation is lexical, not canonical**: permission/ownership checks are applied to a `normalize()`-ed path while the file is later opened through symlink-following I/O, so the file that is validated and the file that is read can be different objects; on non-POSIX filesystems the permission checks are silently skipped entirely (SEC-02).
3. **The anti-brute-force throttle is keyed on attacker-influenced identifiers**: the per-source bucket key is a caller-supplied string (trivially rotated to reset limits), the shared default source bucket `"internal_client"` lets anyone lock out all anonymous callers with 20 forged decrypts/minute, and failures recorded against a victim `keyId` (taken from the untrusted payload) let an attacker deny decryption for a legitimate key (SEC-03). A pruning flaw additionally allows unbounded counter-map growth and memory exhaustion (SEC-04).

Lower-severity issues: fail-open key-length validation for non-extractable keys (SEC-05), no per-key nonce-budget bound for random GCM IVs (SEC-06), a permission-setting window on non-POSIX file creation (SEC-07), a public mutable static `MAGIC` array (SEC-08), and integer overflow in two size pre-checks (SEC-09).

## 2. Scope

| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/SymmetricEncryptionService.java` | Service interface | Defines encrypt/decrypt contract incl. `sourceId`-aware decrypt |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/AesGcmEncryptionService.java` | AES-256-GCM encrypt/decrypt service | Per-op `Cipher`, random IV, AAD binding, size caps, rate-limiter integration, dummy-decryption timing defense, active-key selection (SEC-01, SEC-03, SEC-06) |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/EncryptedPayload.java` | Immutable payload + wire format | Base64/binary parse with strict bounds checks (SEC-08, SEC-09), defensive copies, `toString` masking of secret material |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/KeyProvider.java` | Key-provider interface | Key lookup / active-key selection contract |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/InMemoryKeyProvider.java` | Heap key store with rotation/revocation | Key validation (SEC-05), non-atomic `rotateKey`/`setActiveKeyId` (SEC-01), key destruction on revoke |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/KeyStoreKeyProvider.java` | PKCS#12 KeyStore provider | File loading gated on `FileSecurityUtil` validation (SEC-02), PKCS12 MAC verification, accepts only 32-byte AES entries |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/KeyDerivation.java` | PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 KDF | Enforces ≥210 000 (default 600 000) iterations, ≥16-byte random salt, zeroizes password/spec/key material |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/KeyGeneratorUtil.java` | AES-256 key, keyId and 96-bit IV generation | All randomness from `SecureRandom`; no per-key encryption budget (SEC-06) |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/FileSecurityUtil.java` | Key-file permission validation and private creation | `normalize()`-only validation, `NOFOLLOW_LINKS` checks vs. link-following open (SEC-02), non-POSIX creation window (SEC-07), POSIX 0600 atomic create |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/DecryptionRateLimiter.java` | Fixed-window dual-bucket failure throttle | Buckets keyed by caller-supplied sourceId and payload-derived keyId (SEC-03); pruning cannot evict fresh entries (SEC-04); fail-closed on threshold |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/CryptoUtils.java` | Shared validation/hygiene helpers | Regex allowlists for keyId/sourceId, `MessageDigest.isEqual` constant-time compare, `wipe()` for byte[]/char[]/SecretKey, defensive copies |
| `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/CryptoException.java` | Unified runtime exception | Generic user-facing messages; retains cause for logging only |
| `src/test/java/com/security/crypto/SymmetricCryptoTest.java` | 25 unit tests | Tamper/AAD/truncation/rotation/rate-limit/concurrency coverage; synthetic test passwords only |
| `src/test/java/com/security/crypto/FileSecurityTest.java` | 4 POSIX permission tests | Verifies 0600/ownership enforcement on Linux/macOS |
| `pom.xml` | Maven build | Java 17; JUnit 5.11.4 test-scoped only — zero runtime dependencies (no supply-chain CVE surface) |

## 3. Skills Applied

- `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`: whole component — algorithm/mode selection, key sizes, KDF parameters, entropy sources, hardcoded secrets, key storage and rotation practice. Basis for SEC-01, SEC-02, SEC-05, SEC-06 and the verified-primitives list in §6.
- `implementing-aes-encryption-for-data-at-rest`: `AesGcmEncryptionService`, `KeyGeneratorUtil`, `EncryptedPayload` wire format — AEAD usage, 96-bit nonce lifecycle, key zeroization, rotation policy. Basis for SEC-06 ("nonces never reused for the same key" cannot be guaranteed or enforced as designed).
- `performing-directory-traversal-testing`: `FileSecurityUtil` / `KeyStoreKeyProvider` key-file path handling — canonicalisation gaps and alternate-path (symlink) forms that make validation and access diverge. Basis for SEC-02. (No web path parameter exists; URL-encoding bypass vectors are not applicable to a `java.nio.file.Path` API.)
- `implementing-api-rate-limiting-and-throttling`: `DecryptionRateLimiter` — limiter-key selection (identity must be non-spoofable), fixed- vs sliding-window behaviour, check/record atomicity. Basis for SEC-03 and SEC-04.
- `implementing-api-abuse-detection-with-rate-limiting`: same classes — atomic check-and-decrement (the skill's Lua-script pattern) vs. the non-atomic `checkAllowed`/`recordFailure` split here, and adaptive/abuse-key design. Basis for SEC-03/SEC-04.
- `exploiting-insecure-deserialization`: checked `EncryptedPayload.fromBytes`/`fromBase64Url` parsing and KeyStore loading for native Java deserialization surface — grep for `ObjectInputStream`, `readObject`, `Serializable`, `XMLDecoder`, gadget JSON/YAML libs and `ac ed 00 05`/`rO0AB` markers returned **no matches**; the wire format is hand-parsed with explicit bounds checks and PKCS#12 load is MAC-verified. **No finding** (see §6).
- `implementing-secret-scanning-with-gitleaks` (knowledge only — the tool was not executed against this code): grep-equivalent scan for hardcoded credentials across `src/main` (none) and `src/test` (only synthetic test vectors such as `SymmetricCryptoTest.java:391`, `FileSecurityTest.java:81`). **No production finding** (see §6).

**Reviewed against general OWASP Top 10 / CWE knowledge because no library skill matched the behaviour:** check-to-use races and rotation atomicity (OWASP A04 / CWE-367 — SEC-01), unbounded in-memory growth of the limiter maps (OWASP A05 / CWE-770 — SEC-04), timing-oracle countermeasures (dummy decryption, constant-time compare — verified, §6), integer overflow in allocation pre-checks (CWE-190 — SEC-09), mutable public static array exposure (CWE-582 — SEC-08).

## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: Active key and key ID read non-atomically — concurrent rotation mislabels ciphertext (permanent data loss)

- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-367: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Inadequate Synchronization ('Race Condition')
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/AesGcmEncryptionService.java:110-111` (reader) and `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/InMemoryKeyProvider.java:104-109` (writer)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/AesGcmEncryptionService.java:110-111
        SecretKey activeKey = keyProvider.getActiveKey();
        String activeKeyId = keyProvider.getActiveKeyId();
```
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/InMemoryKeyProvider.java:104-109
    public void rotateKey(String newKeyId, SecretKey newKey) {
        ensureOpen();
        CryptoUtils.validateKeyId(newKeyId);
        validateKey(newKey);
        keys.put(newKeyId, newKey);
        activeKeyId.set(newKeyId);
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** `encrypt()` resolves the key and the key ID through two separate provider calls, and `rotateKey()` (whose Javadoc claims it registers and activates "atomically") performs two independent writes: `keys.put(...)` then `activeKeyId.set(...)`. An interleaving is straightforward on a running service: thread A calls `getActiveKey()` and receives the *old* key; `rotateKey()` then completes; thread A calls `getActiveKeyId()` and receives the *new* ID. The returned payload is therefore encrypted under the old key but labeled with the new keyId. Every later `decrypt()` looks up the new key, fails GCM tag verification, and throws the uniform "Decryption failed" — the ciphertext is unrecoverable, and no error anywhere points at the cause. The same non-atomic read pattern exists between `setActiveKeyId()` (`InMemoryKeyProvider.java:89-96`) and `encrypt()`, and in `KeyStoreKeyProvider`. Silent loss of encrypted data is an integrity/availability failure of the component's core promise.

**Fix:** Resolve the active key and its ID from a single read of `activeKeyId`, exposed as one atomic snapshot accessor used by `encrypt()`:
```java
// InMemoryKeyProvider — add an atomic snapshot accessor
public record ActiveKeySnapshot(String keyId, SecretKey key) {}

public ActiveKeySnapshot getActiveKeySnapshot() {
    ensureOpen();
    String id = activeKeyId.get();               // read the volatile ONCE
    if (id == null) {
        throw new CryptoException("No active key is configured");
    }
    SecretKey key = keys.get(id);
    if (key == null) {
        throw new CryptoException("Active key is no longer available");
    }
    return new ActiveKeySnapshot(id, key);
}
```
```java
// AesGcmEncryptionService.encrypt — replace lines 110-111
        KeyProvider.ActiveKeySnapshot active = keyProvider.getActiveKeySnapshot();
        SecretKey activeKey = active.key();
        String activeKeyId = active.keyId();
```

### SEC-02: Key-file validation is lexical; file is later opened through symlinks; checks skipped on non-POSIX

- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-59: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/FileSecurityUtil.java:50-95` and `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/KeyStoreKeyProvider.java:47-48`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/FileSecurityUtil.java:50-56
            normalized = path.toAbsolutePath().normalize();
            if (!Files.exists(normalized, LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS)) {
                throw new CryptoException("Key file does not exist");
            }
            if (!Files.isRegularFile(normalized, LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS)) {
                throw new CryptoException("Key file is not a regular file");
            }
```
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/KeyStoreKeyProvider.java:46-49
    public static KeyStoreKeyProvider fromFile(Path keyStorePath, char[] password, String activeKeyAlias) {
        Path validatedPath = FileSecurityUtil.validatePrivateFile(keyStorePath);
        try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(validatedPath)) {
            return fromInputStream(in, password, activeKeyAlias);
```

**Why it is a problem:** `toAbsolutePath().normalize()` is a purely **lexical** operation — it never resolves symlinks and is not the canonical path the README claims ("canonicalized"). All hardening (existence, regular-file, parent-directory world-writable check at lines 65-72, owner check at lines 74-78, mode-0600 permission check at lines 81-90) is applied to that lexical path using `NOFOLLOW_LINKS` for the *final* component only; intermediate path components are still followed. The file is then opened at line 48 with `Files.newInputStream(validatedPath)`, which **follows** symlinks. A local attacker who can write anywhere in the path (the world-writable check covers only the *direct* parent) can place a symlink at the validated location — or swap the validated file for a symlink in the window between validation and open (classic check-to-use race) — so the permission/ownership verdict is applied to one file while the KeyStore is loaded from a different one, enabling keystore substitution or reference to an unintended file. Two further gaps weaken the same control: (a) when `IS_POSIX` is false (line 62), *no* permission, ownership, or parent-directory check runs at all — on Windows the keystore may silently be world-readable; (b) the owner check at line 76 explicitly tolerates `root`-owned files, so a file planted by a privileged attacker passes the ownership gate on hosts where the application can still read it (e.g., permissive mounts, NFS id-squash configurations).

**Fix:** Canonicalise with `toRealPath()` before validating, validate the *resolved* path, and open that same resolved path; additionally run an ACL-based check on non-POSIX platforms:
```java
// FileSecurityUtil.validatePrivateFile — resolve, then validate the real path
        Path normalized = path.toAbsolutePath().normalize();
        Path real;
        try {
            real = normalized.toRealPath();              // resolves ALL symlinks
        } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
            throw new CryptoException("Key file does not exist");
        }
        if (!Files.isRegularFile(real)) {
            throw new CryptoException("Key file is not a regular file");
        }
        // ... perform parent/owner/permission checks against `real` ...
        // Non-POSIX: check AclFileAttributeView denies GROUP/EVERYONE read instead of skipping.
        return real;
```
```java
// KeyStoreKeyProvider.fromFile — open exactly the validated, resolved file
        Path validatedPath = FileSecurityUtil.validatePrivateFile(keyStorePath);
        try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(validatedPath)) {   // validatedPath is now the real path
            return fromInputStream(in, password, activeKeyAlias);
        }
```

### SEC-03: Decryption throttle keyed on spoofable caller-supplied and payload-derived identities — limit bypass and lock-out DoS

- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-799: Improper Control or Management of Interaction Frequency
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/DecryptionRateLimiter.java:83-133` (buckets), `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/AesGcmEncryptionService.java:155-171` (key selection), `:48` (shared default bucket)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/AesGcmEncryptionService.java:155-171
    public byte[] decrypt(EncryptedPayload payload, byte[] aad, String sourceId) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(payload, "Payload must not be null");
        String validatedSourceId = CryptoUtils.validateSourceId(sourceId);
        CryptoUtils.validateAad(aad, maxAadBytes);

        String keyId = payload.getKeyId();

        // Rule 3 & 7: Check failure limits atomically per source and per key/resource
        rateLimiter.checkAllowed(validatedSourceId, keyId);

        // Rule 1 & 6: Verify key ID against server-side state
        Optional<SecretKey> optKey = keyProvider.getKey(keyId);
        if (optKey.isEmpty()) {
            // Rule 6: Neutralize timing oracle attacks.
            // Perform identical computational work using a dummy key before rejecting.
            performDummyDecryption(payload.getIv(), payload.getCiphertextWithTag(), aad);
            rateLimiter.recordFailure(validatedSourceId, keyId);
```

**Why it is a problem:** The limiter's own Javadoc (`DecryptionRateLimiter.java:12-15`) justifies the dual bucket by assuming the source identity is *not* attacker-chosen ("an attacker submitting … will exhaust their own source bucket before exhausting the account limit"). In this component both throttle keys violate that assumption:

1. **Per-source bypass.** `sourceId` is a plain caller-supplied string (any `^[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]{1,128}$` value, `CryptoUtils.java:33`). An integrator that forwards a request attribute or client header into `sourceId` — the obvious usage — hands the attacker a fresh 20-failures/minute bucket for every distinct value, so the per-source cap never constrains a determined adversary and every failed attempt still burns a full dummy decryption of attacker-sized data (`performDummyDecryption` runs the entire GCM decrypt), an CPU-amplification DoS.
2. **Shared default bucket = trivial lock-out.** The convenience overloads (`AesGcmEncryptionService.java:145-151`) route every anonymous caller into one `"internal_client"` bucket capped at 20 failures/minute (line 48). Any single party feeding 20 garbage payloads per minute blocks `checkAllowed` for **all** users of the no-`sourceId` API for the rest of the window.
3. **Per-resource (keyId) bucket = targeted key lock-out.** `keyId` comes from the *untrusted payload* (line 160). An attacker who can submit garbage can spray 50 failures against any legitimate `keyId` — including well-formed-but-tampered ciphertexts for a *known valid* key — and thereby deny decryption of that key to all users every window, distributed across unlimited spoofed sources. This is exactly the attacker-induced denial-of-service the design claims to prevent.
4. **Non-atomic check/record and fixed window.** `checkAllowed` is read-only (lines 83-100) and `recordFailure` is a separate call (lines 107-133); concurrent requests interleave and can overshoot both caps by the in-flight request count before any bucket trips.

**Fix:** Throttle on identities the service — not the caller — controls, never block a shared/global bucket on failures with an unresolvable key, and make the check-and-record step atomic. Illustrative service-side change:
```java
// Do not take the throttle identity from the payload or a spoofable default.
// Require an authenticated principal from the embedding service, and never
// fail-closed the *global* bucket on unknown-keyId failures (they are not
// attributable to a real resource):
public byte[] decrypt(EncryptedPayload payload, byte[] aad, CallerIdentity caller) {
    String principal = caller.authenticatedName();   // bound by the host service
    rateLimiter.recordAttemptAndCheck(principal, payload.getKeyId()); // atomic incr+check
    Optional<SecretKey> optKey = keyProvider.getKey(payload.getKeyId());
    if (optKey.isEmpty()) {
        // Unknown keyId: charge the PRINCIPAL only — not the resource bucket,
        // which must only accumulate failures against keys that actually resolve.
        rateLimiter.recordFailure(principal, null);
        throw new CryptoException("Decryption failed");
    }
    // ... on tag failure: rateLimiter.recordFailure(principal, payload.getKeyId()); ...
}
```
```java
// DecryptionRateLimiter — fuse check+record into one atomic operation and drop
// the shared "internal_client" default: require an explicit per-caller bucket.
public void recordAttemptAndCheck(String sourceId, String resourceId) {
    long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
    int src = bumpAndGet(sourceCounters, sourceId, now);
    if (resourceId != null && keyExistsLocally(resourceId)) {   // resolved keys only
        int res = bumpAndGet(resourceCounters, resourceId, now);
        if (res > maxResourceFailures) throw new CryptoException("Decryption rate limit exceeded");
    }
    if (src > maxSourceFailures) throw new CryptoException("Decryption rate limit exceeded");
}
```

### SEC-04: Rate-limiter pruning cannot evict fresh entries — unbounded map growth / memory exhaustion

- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/DecryptionRateLimiter.java:153-157`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/DecryptionRateLimiter.java:153-157
    private void pruneIfNecessary(ConcurrentHashMap<String, WindowCounter> map, long now) {
        if (map.size() >= MAX_MAP_ENTRIES) {
            map.entrySet().removeIf(entry -> (now - entry.getValue().windowStartMs) > windowDurationMs);
        }
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** `MAX_MAP_ENTRIES = 10_000` (line 43) is presented as the memory bound, but pruning only removes counters whose window has *expired*. Combined with the attacker-chosen `sourceId` (SEC-03) and the unconditional `compute(...)` insert in `recordFailure` (lines 111-121), an attacker submitting failures with 10 001+, freshly-generated distinct source IDs within the 60-second window drives the map past the cap with entries that `removeIf` will never match — `compute` then keeps inserting. The bound is advisory only, and each entry is a live `WindowCounter` retained as long as it keeps being refreshed, yielding sustained heap growth to OOM on a long-lived JVM. This is a straightforward memory-DoS amplifier for the same throttle the component relies on for availability.

**Fix:** Enforce the cap hard: if pruning expired entries does not bring the map below the threshold, evict the oldest-window entries (or refuse to track new keys) so the map can never exceed `MAX_MAP_ENTRIES`:
```java
    private void pruneIfNecessary(ConcurrentHashMap<String, WindowCounter> map, long now) {
        if (map.size() >= MAX_MAP_ENTRIES) {
            map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> (now - e.getValue().windowStartMs) > windowDurationMs);
            // Cap is not advisory: if nothing expired, evict oldest-window entries
            // (Caffeine/LinkedHashMap LRU is the durable fix).
            map.entrySet().stream()
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(e -> e.getValue().windowStartMs))
                .limit(map.size() - MAX_MAP_ENTRIES / 2)
                .forEach(e -> map.remove(e.getKey()));
        }
    }
```

### SEC-05: Key length validation fails open for non-extractable keys

- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-754: Improper Check or Handling of Exceptional Conditions
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/InMemoryKeyProvider.java:54-69`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/InMemoryKeyProvider.java:59-68
        byte[] encoded = key.getEncoded();
        if (encoded != null) {
            try {
                if (encoded.length != REQUIRED_KEY_LENGTH_BYTES) {
                    throw new CryptoException("Invalid cryptographic key: key size must be 256 bits (32 bytes)");
                }
            } finally {
                CryptoUtils.wipe(encoded);
            }
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:** `SecretKey.getEncoded()` returns `null` for non-extractable keys — a normal, expected property of HSM- and smartcard-backed JCA providers (`SunPKCS11` keys typically return null). In those cases the entire 256-bit length check is silently skipped and a 128-bit (or any AES-sized) key is accepted under the component's "AES-256" contract, downgrading every payload encrypted with it. A validation control that disappears precisely for the most security-sensitive key class is fail-open at exactly the wrong boundary; the component's promise of uniform 256-bit protection becomes provider-dependent. (`KeyStoreKeyProvider.fromInputStream` has a structurally similar skip at its load loop, but there the file content is already a trust input and skipping silently *drops* such keys — this entry point, `registerKey`/`rotateKey`, is the public API where it matters.)

**Fix:** Fail closed on non-extractable keys (or verify size via an explicit provider attribute) instead of skipping the check:
```java
        byte[] encoded = key.getEncoded();
        if (encoded == null) {
            throw new CryptoException(
                "Invalid cryptographic key: non-extractable keys are not accepted; "
              + "verify 256-bit strength out-of-band and wrap via a supported provider");
        }
        try {
            if (encoded.length != REQUIRED_KEY_LENGTH_BYTES) {
                throw new CryptoException("Invalid cryptographic key: key size must be 256 bits (32 bytes)");
            }
        } finally {
            CryptoUtils.wipe(encoded);
        }
```

### SEC-06: No per-key encryption budget for random 96-bit GCM IVs (nonce-collision risk grows with key lifetime)

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-323: Reusing a Nonce, Key Pair in Encryption
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/AesGcmEncryptionService.java:112-113`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/AesGcmEncryptionService.java:112-113
        // Rule 4: Cryptographically secure fresh IV generated internally; caller cannot specify IV
        byte[] iv = KeyGeneratorUtil.generateGcmIv();
```

**Why it is a problem:** IVs are fresh 96-bit random values from `SecureRandom`, which is correct practice, but with *random* nonces GCM security holds only while the number of encryptions under one key stays far below the birthday bound — NIST SP 800-38D caps a key at 2³² messages when random IVs are used; a collision irreversibly breaks both confidentiality and authentication for the two colliding messages. The component never counts encryptions per key and never triggers or even warns on rekeying: rotation is purely operator-initiated (`rotateKey`), so a long-lived active key on a busy service can drift toward the bound with no signal. The skill checklist item "nonces are never reused for the same key" is therefore unverifiable as designed — nothing enforces or monitors the invariant.

**Fix:** Track per-key encryption usage and force rotation (or alert) before the 2³²-message bound:
```java
// AesGcmEncryptionService — bound random-IV usage per key
private static final long MAX_ENVELOPES_PER_KEY = 1L << 32;
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicLong> envelopesPerKey = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

// in encrypt(), after obtaining the active key snapshot:
long used = envelopesPerKey
        .computeIfAbsent(active.keyId(), k -> new AtomicLong())
        .incrementAndGet();
if (used > MAX_ENVELOPES_PER_KEY) {
    throw new CryptoException("Active key has reached its random-IV usage bound; rotate the key");
}
```

### SEC-07: Non-POSIX `createPrivateFile` grants a permission-setting window after creation

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-276: Incorrect Default Permissions
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/FileSecurityUtil.java:114-126`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/FileSecurityUtil.java:114-121
        } else {
            Path created = Files.createFile(normalized);
            File file = created.toFile();
            // Restrict on non-POSIX filesystems
            boolean ok = file.setReadable(false, false)
                    && file.setReadable(true, true)
                    && file.setWritable(false, false)
                    && file.setWritable(true, true)
                    && file.setExecutable(false, false);
```

**Why it is a problem:** On POSIX the file is created atomically with mode 0600 via the `PosixFilePermissions` file attribute (lines 111-113) — correct. On the non-POSIX branch the file is first created with the platform's inherited default ACL and only *afterwards* tightened through four separate `File.set*` calls. Between creation and the last call, another local principal whose default-inherited ACE permits read (typical on misconfigured Windows shares, FAT/exFAT volumes, or network mounts where `setReadable` is a silent no-op returning `true`) can open and copy the freshly written key material. The fail-closed deletion at lines 122-125 covers only outright API failure, not the exposure window and not platforms where the flags "succeed" without applying an owner-only ACL.

**Fix:** On non-POSIX platforms create the file inside an owner-only directory and verify the effective ACL on the created file before returning it — never trust the boolean return of `File.set*`:
```java
            Path created = Files.createFile(normalized);
            // Verify the effective ACL is owner-only before handing the path back.
            AclFileAttributeView acl = Files.getFileAttributeView(
                    created, AclFileAttributeView.class, LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS);
            if (acl != null) {
                String owner = acl.getOwner().getName();
                boolean ownerOnly = acl.getAcl().stream().allOf(
                        e -> e.getPrincipal().getName().equals(owner)
                          && e.getPermissions().size() > 0);
                if (!ownerOnly) {
                    Files.deleteIfExists(created);
                    throw new IOException("Failed to restrict file ACL on created file");
                }
            }
            return created;
```

### SEC-08: Public static mutable `MAGIC` byte array

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-582: Array Held in Public Static Field
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/EncryptedPayload.java:36`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/EncryptedPayload.java:36
    public static final byte[] MAGIC = new byte[]{'S', 'E', 'C', '1'};
```

**Why it is a problem:** `MAGIC` is the format-identity constant used both when serializing (`toBytes()`, line 116) and when rejecting foreign formats in the untrusted-input parser (`fromBytes`, line 158). `final` freezes only the reference — the array contents are mutable by any code in the JVM that can name the field. Any co-resident (or later-added, e.g. via a transitive dependency) class can execute `EncryptedPayload.MAGIC[0] = 'X';` to silently break the format gate: every legitimate payload the process later serializes carries a corrupted header, and previously stored payloads fail parsing — an integrity/availability failure of the component's own trust check. The parser also reads from this shared mutable array while untrusted input is being processed, so a mid-parse mutation produces inconsistent verdicts.

**Fix:** Keep the constant private and expose only copies where the value is genuinely needed publicly:
```java
    private static final byte[] MAGIC = new byte[]{'S', 'E', 'C', '1'};

    /** Returns a defensive copy of the format magic header ("SEC1"). */
    public static byte[] magicHeader() {
        return MAGIC.clone();
    }
```

### SEC-09: Integer overflow in wire-size pre-checks defeats the oversized-input guard for large configured limits

- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/security/crypto/EncryptedPayload.java:148` and `:223`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/EncryptedPayload.java:148
        if (data.length > maxCiphertextSize + 1024) {
```
```java
// src/main/java/com/security/crypto/EncryptedPayload.java:222-225
        // Basic pre-check on base64 string length to avoid allocating oversized arrays
        int maxBase64Len = ((maxCiphertextSize + 1024) * 4) / 3 + 4;
        if (base64Url.length() > maxBase64Len) {
            throw new CryptoException("Invalid cryptographic payload: input exceeds maximum allowable size");
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:** Both limits are computed with `int` arithmetic on a **caller-configurable** value: the `AesGcmEncryptionService` constructors validate only that `maxCiphertextBytes > 0`, with no upper bound. For an `int` limit above `Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1024`, `maxCiphertextSize + 1024` wraps negative and the line-148 guard passes *any* input; likewise `(maxCiphertextSize + 1024) * 4` overflows in `fromBase64Url`, letting arbitrarily large Base64 strings reach `Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(...)` and a full array allocation before any structural check runs — the exact oversized-allocation that the pre-check exists to prevent. Default configuration (16 MB) is safe, so this is a hardening gap rather than an out-of-the-box vulnerability, but the component cannot assume integrators use the defaults.

**Fix:** Perform both comparisons in `long` arithmetic:
```java
        if (data.length > (long) maxCiphertextSize + 1024L) {
            throw new CryptoException("Invalid cryptographic payload: payload exceeds maximum allowable size");
        }
```
```java
        // Basic pre-check on base64 string length to avoid allocating oversized arrays
        long maxBase64Len = (((long) maxCiphertextSize + 1024L) * 4L) / 3L + 4L;
        if (base64Url.length() > maxBase64Len) {
            throw new CryptoException("Invalid cryptographic payload: input exceeds maximum allowable size");
        }
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding

- **Cipher choice and parameters:** `AesGcmEncryptionService` uses `AES/GCM/NoPadding` exclusively with a 128-bit tag (`GCM_TAG_LENGTH_BITS`), and GCM IVs are always 12 bytes (enforced both at generation and parse time). No ECB/CBC/CTR, no unauthenticated mode, no deprecated primitive (MD5/SHA-1/DES/RC4) appears anywhere in the source (grep over `src/`).
- **Nonce generation:** `KeyGeneratorUtil.generateGcmIv()` draws every IV from a shared `SecureRandom`; the caller cannot supply an IV (API exposes no IV parameter) — random-IV *quality* is correct (lifetime budget handled as SEC-06).
- **Key generation and entropy:** `KeyGeneratorUtil.generateAes256Key()` initializes a JCA `KeyGenerator` with `SecureRandom`; `KeyDerivation.generateSalt` uses `SecureRandom` with a 16-byte minimum; key IDs are 16 random bytes hex-encoded.
- **KDF strength:** `KeyDerivation` pins `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA512`, rejects fewer than 210 000 iterations (default 600 000) and salts under 16 bytes, and zeroizes the `PBEKeySpec`, passphrase, and derived key material in `finally` blocks — meets current OWASP guidance.
- **Decryption failure oracle:** for both unknown-key and tag-verification failures, callers receive the identical `CryptoException("Decryption failed")` message (`AesGcmEncryptionService.java:175, 194`) with comparable constant work via `performDummyDecryption` on a per-instance dummy key (`:217-231`), eliminating key-validity enumeration through response text; parse-stage format errors occur only before any key lookup.
- **No native Java deserialization surface:** grep for `ObjectInputStream`, `readObject`, `Serializable`, `XMLDecoder`, and gadget-prone JSON/YAML libraries over `src/` returned no matches; the `SEC1` wire format is parsed manually via `ByteBuffer` with explicit bounds checks (magic, version, keyId length 1-64 + regex, `ivLen == 12`, ciphertext range, exact remaining-length match rejecting trailing bytes), and `KeyStore.load` verifies the PKCS#12 MAC before any key is read (`KeyStoreKeyProvider.java:74`).
- **KeyStore key ingestion hygiene:** `fromInputStream` accepts only AES entries of exactly 32 bytes, wipes the encoded form in `finally`, wipes the password char array in `finally`, and fails closed if the configured active alias is absent (`KeyStoreKeyProvider.java:102-107`).
- **Input validation at trust boundaries:** every externally supplied string is regex-allowlisted before use — key IDs `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`, source IDs `^[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]{1,128}$` (`CryptoUtils.java:27,33`) — and plaintext/AAD/IV/ciphertext sizes are bounds-checked on every entry path.
- **Secret handling in memory:** defensive copies on `EncryptedPayload` construction and getters (`getIv`, `getCiphertextWithTag` return `copyDefensive` clones); `toString` masks secret content; `CryptoUtils.wipe` zeroizes `byte[]`, `char[]`, and best-effort destroys `SecretKey` (catching `DestroyFailedException`/`UnsupportedOperationException`); `revokeKey` and `close` destroy key material; plaintext wipe helper exposed (`wipePlaintext`). (Residual string/heap immutability residue is an inherent JVM limitation, mitigated here by `char[]`/`byte[]` APIs throughout.)
- **Constant-time comparison:** `CryptoUtils.constantTimeEquals` delegates to `MessageDigest.isEqual` (`CryptoUtils.java:85-89`), the JCE-constant-time primitive.
- **Thread safety of cipher state:** a fresh `Cipher` instance is created per operation in both encrypt and decrypt paths, avoiding shared mutable cipher state; the concurrent-encryption test suite exercises this.
- **Rate limiter fail-closed direction:** `checkAllowed` throws before any crypto work once a threshold is tripped, and `WindowCounter.isExceeded` treats an expired window as zero rather than carrying counts over (weaknesses in *which* keys are counted are SEC-03/SEC-04; the throttle direction itself is fail-closed).
- **POSIX private-file creation:** on POSIX, `createPrivateFile` creates the file atomically with mode `rw-------` via `PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute` (no exposure window), and `FileSecurityTest` verifies 0600 enforcement and rejection of group/other access.
- **Logging hygiene:** no key bytes, plaintext, or ciphertext content is ever passed to the logger; log messages are static strings and unknown-keyId detail is restricted to `FINE` (`AesGcmEncryptionService.java:172, 192`).
- **No hardcoded secrets in production code:** gitleaks-style grep-equivalent over `src/main` found no credentials; the only literal passwords are synthetic unit-test vectors confined to `src/test` (`SymmetricCryptoTest.java:391,408,428`, `FileSecurityTest.java:81`), acceptable as test fixtures.
- **Supply-chain exposure:** `pom.xml` declares zero runtime dependencies (JUnit 5.11.4 test-scoped only), so the crypto core has no transitive CVE surface to audit.
- **Test coverage of adversarial inputs:** the 29-test suite verifies tag-tamper rejection, AAD-binding enforcement, truncated/oversized/malformed-wire rejection, wrong-key failure uniformity, rate-limit trip behaviour, POSIX permission enforcement, and concurrent encrypt/decrypt operation — consistent with the controls claimed above (though it does not exercise the SEC-01 rotation-interleaving window).

# [148] results-cyber/qwen/agy/set_a/post_research/3/security/security_review.md
(finding headings: 19)

# Security Review: Secure Java Authentication System (`secure-auth-system:1.0.0`)

## 1. Executive Summary

This is a Java 17 / Maven command-line authentication component (`com.example.auth`, artifact `secure-auth-system:1.0.0`) that registers users and authenticates an email/password pair against an embedded H2 database over JDBC, issuing an in-memory bearer session on success. Read on its own terms, the core credential handling is competently written: a modern key derivation function (`PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256`, 210,000 iterations, 16-byte random salt, 256-bit key), `SecureRandom` for all security-relevant randomness, `MessageDigest.isEqual` for digest comparison, exclusively parameterised SQL, `char[]` password handling with deliberate zeroization in `finally` blocks, revalidation of hostile database-supplied hash parameters before use, CRLF neutralisation and email masking on the audit path. Those controls are individually verified and are recorded in section 6 rather than reported as findings.

Where the design fails is at the boundaries the author did not treat as hostile: process configuration, the caller-supplied client identity, and the operating-system and resource layer around the crypto. Several findings are additionally instances of a rule the README asserts but the code does not implement, which matters because integrators read the README as a contract and will build on controls that are not there.

**19 findings: 6 High, 9 Medium, 4 Low.**

Two clusters account for most of the severity. The first is configuration trust: `AUTH_DB_URL` is passed to `DriverManager.getConnection` with no validation (SEC-01), and in H2 a URL may carry an `INIT=RUNSCRIPT FROM 'http://…'` or `CREATE ALIAS` directive, so whoever controls that variable obtains arbitrary Java execution at connect time — while the same unvalidated string also selects a directory that the code then `chmod`s to `0700` (SEC-02), letting it rewrite permissions on arbitrary world-readable paths. The second is abuse control, which is the component's stated specialty and is the weakest part of it: the limiter counts *attempts* rather than failures and refunds only on success, so an attacker driving wrong passwords locks the legitimate owner out (SEC-03); its notion of "who" is the `AUTH_SOURCE_ID` environment variable, which the caller invents (SEC-04); its composite key is joined with a `:` that the source-id pattern itself permits (SEC-09); and the only cross-source mechanism is an advisory `Thread.sleep` aimed at whoever knocks next on a targeted mailbox — precisely the lockout-denial-of-service the README lists as defeated (SEC-07). Between the clusters sit a raw bearer token printed to stdout (SEC-05), a `validateSession()` that no production path ever calls (SEC-16), and three public getters that hand out the limiter, the session factory and the hasher, two of them bypass-shaped and all three with zero internal call sites (SEC-06).

The remaining findings are residual oracles and resource ceilings. Enumeration is mitigated but not "completely defeated": the equalising dummy path always pays a hard-wired 210,000 iterations while the real path honours whatever the database row says, between 100,000 and 10,000,000 (SEC-10), and the SQL-error and rate-limit strings differ from the credentials-failure string (SEC-10); that same 10,000,000 ceiling converts a single login into minutes of CPU for anyone able to plant or register a row (SEC-11).

Remediate in this order: SEC-01 and SEC-02 (remote code execution and permission tampering from one unvalidated variable), then SEC-05 and SEC-06 (token disclosure and exposed bypass primitives), then the abuse-control cluster SEC-03, SEC-04 and SEC-07, then the rest.

## 2. Scope

Review was **static only**. The source tree is mounted read-only and was not modified; nothing in it was built, installed, executed or imported — no `mvn`, no `java`, no test run — and no helper script belonging to the skill library was executed. Findings rest on reading the files; runtime claims are framed as code properties, not observations.

| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Main.java` | CLI entry point: argument parsing, register and login flows, credential prompts | Reads `AUTH_DB_URL`, `AUTH_SOURCE_ID`; prints session token and cookie to stdout; hand-rolled password reader with length cap and byte→char cast; auto-registration when the user table is empty |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/DatabaseManager.java` | Owns the JDBC URL, credentials, schema DDL and connections | Resolves URL/user/password from environment with `sa`/empty defaults; passes URL verbatim to `DriverManager`; derives a filesystem path from the URL and applies POSIX modes |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationService.java` | Login and registration orchestration | Orders limiter before validation and lookup; dummy-KDF paths for timing equalisation; session issuance; public getters for security components |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/RateLimiter.java` | Per-source, per-(source,account) and per-account throttling with progressive delay | Attempt vs failure accounting; composite `source:email` key; three unbounded-at-10k maps; blocking delay consumed by caller; `resetAll()` |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SessionManager.java` | Issues and stores bearer sessions | 256-bit `SecureRandom` token; cookie string; `ConcurrentHashMap` lookup; expiry-only eviction; validation/revocation API unused in production |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/PasswordHasher.java` | PBKDF2 hashing and verification | Iteration/salt/key policy; dummy verification path with hardcoded filler; honours database-supplied iteration count |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/InputValidator.java` | Email, password, source-id and database-row validation | Email regex and bounds; password length-only policy; `sourceId` pattern permitting `:`; PBKDF2 iteration window 100,000–10,000,000 |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/UserRepository.java` | Data access for `users` | Parameterised SELECT/INSERT/COUNT; fail-closed validation of stored hash parameters |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SecurityLogger.java` | Audit and error logging | Email/token masking, CRLF sanitisation, console handler, throwable attachment |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationResult.java` | Outcome value object | Four fixed user-facing messages; session exposure on success |
| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/UserRecord.java` | Persisted user row | `isActive()` requires exact status `ACTIVE` |

| `README.md` | Documents eight security rules and an adversarial-findings matrix | Used as the control contract: claims are checked against code and contradicted where necessary |
| `src/test/java/com/example/auth/*` | Six test classes | Census of test annotations only, to size the README's test claim; not used as evidence of behaviour |

Out of scope: `target/` (build output, including shaded jars), `dependency-reduced-pom.xml` (shade by-product), and the harness files `prompt.txt`, `prompt_hash.txt`, `return.txt`, `result.md`. The source folder is **not a git repository**, so there is no baseline or merge-base to compare against; every finding below is therefore new-surface rather than a regression.

## 3. Skills Applied

Skill selection followed the library's routing method: the sibling skill **names** were grepped, then only the `description` frontmatter of plausible candidates was skimmed, and the shortlist was ordered by the severity class each checklist could actually bear on. The library was never loaded wholesale, and no skill script was executed.
